T1: Owners of campers, vans and caravans already know the Eberspaecher heater brand (Airtronic, Hydronic) and would buy a retrofit or upgraded heater if it were sold through the installer and accessory channels they already use. The company could earn margin by selling a branded aftermarket kit through those channels rather than by building a new consumer brand. Who benefits: Eberspaecher (aftermarket margin on existing heater technology) and van-conversion installers who gain a recognised product.. Why behaviour changes: Recognition of the brand from its use in OEM and dealer-fitted heaters lowers the trust barrier. Owners who already want winter comfort for camping or van life will pay for a known name over an unknown one.. How value is captured: Branded aftermarket kits and installer-channel margin on units that reuse the existing heater platform, with little new product development.. Assumptions: Individual owners currently buy heaters mainly through installers or specialist retail, not direct from Eberspaecher; Brand recognition from OEM fitment transfers to purchase intent in the aftermarket; Installer margins leave room for a premium-priced branded kit. Predictions: Aftermarket sell-through rises where installers display the Eberspaecher name on the kit; Owners who name a brand at purchase choose Eberspaecher above unbranded or Asian alternatives at equal price; Installers report unprompted requests for the brand, as the booth interview suggests.

T2: Individual buyers do not switch to a heater brand on recognition alone. The installer or dealer chooses the heater and holds the customer relationship, so a direct consumer proposition captures little value unless the company controls the installation and service point. Who benefits: Installers and specialist dealers, who keep the margin and the customer. Eberspaecher benefits only if it can capture that channel.. Why behaviour changes: Buyers rely on the installer's recommendation and fitting quality, not on the component brand. The switching point is installation and after-sales service, so the party that controls those gains the sale.. How value is captured: Only through owning or contracting the installation and service network, or by supplying the installer at trade prices. A brand-led kit sold direct would capture little.. Assumptions: Most individual heater purchases are made with an installer or dealer involved; Installers choose the product on fit, warranty and margin, not on component brand; Eberspaecher has no installation network of its own to exploit. Predictions: Share of heater sales made direct to owners is low, and most sales run through installers; Installers offer whichever heater they can fit and warrant most easily, not the most recognised; A direct-to-consumer kit without installer support sells poorly relative to installer-fitted units.

T1 supports, from eberspaecher-booth-owners (company_assertion): ""People simply know the Airtronic and Hydronic, many have them installed in their own camper or car."". Does not show: This is the company's own trade-fair statement, not measured awareness or purchase intent. It does not show how many owners buy direct, what share is aftermarket, or whether recognition converts to sales at a premium price..

T2 neutral, from ec-parking-heater-duopoly (regulation): "Webasto and Eberspächer are the only suppliers of fuel-operated parking heaters and fuel-operated auxiliary heaters for cars and trucks in the EEA.". It says nothing about how individual buyers choose a heater, whether installers decide the purchase, or who holds the customer relationship today. It is neutral for T2, though it does show a concentrated market in which a direct channel is not obviously blocked..

Does not show: This is an Australian consumer-advice article, not sales data. It shows that price gaps pull owners towards cheap units, which weakens the assumption that brand recognition earns a premium. It does not show the size of the gap, the share of buyers involved, or how European buyers choose..

Test "Installer-channel branded kit price test" between T1; T2. Method: Offer a branded Eberspaecher-labelled retrofit kit for a common camper-van heater model through three to five independent van-conversion installers and two online accessory retailers, at three price points (proposed: standard, +10%, +20% over the unbranded equivalent). Track listings, enquiries and fitted units. Compare with an unbranded equivalent listed alongside it.. Sample: Proposed: 4 installers and 2 online retailers in Germany, each listing both branded and unbranded units for 10 weeks; estimated 300 to 500 listing-days of exposure.. Measure: Share of buyers choosing the branded kit at each price point; number of unprompted installer requests naming the brand; share of sales routed through installers versus direct online.. Predictions: T1: Branded kit takes a meaningful share, and holds share at a +10% premium, because owners pay for a known name.; T2: Choice follows the installer's recommendation; branded kit sells mainly where installers fit it, and direct online sales of the branded kit are low regardless of brand recognition.. Decision rule: Proceed to a direct aftermarket proposition only if the branded kit holds at least 30 percent of unit sales at +10% price premium where it is offered, AND at least half of its sales come through channels the company can reach without relying on installers' own recommendation. If branded share falls below 15 percent at +10%, or installers control more than 80 percent of the sale, stop and keep a B2B or installer-supply posture.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.
Looked for evidence against T2: "parking heater owners buy online direct without installer self-install retail"; found rvdaily-owners-tempted, ec-parking-heater-duopoly, iims-boat-owner-diy.

T2 contradicts, from iims-boat-owner-diy (customer_observation): "They are being fitted by owners of boats, many of whom will not be aware of the strict requirements for correct installation.". Does not show: This is a UK marine surveyors' warning about boats, not road vehicles or campers, and it does not give sales volumes or the share of owners who self-fit. It shows owners sometimes bypass installers, which weakens the claim that installers always control the purchase. It does not show that owners buy direct from the manufacturer..

Favours T2: Do not build a direct consumer proposition now. The evidence so far is thin: the company's own booth remark suggests some brand recognition among camper owners, but the price-led and owner self-fitting evidence cuts against both a recognition premium (T1) and installer control (T2). Keep the core business as a B2B supplier to OEMs and specialist dealers. If the company wants to test the consumer case, run the low-cost installer and price test first, and treat installer control and price sensitivity as the two things it must measure. Beliefs: T1: unlikely; T2: uncertain.

T2 kept: SYN-D is a SIMULATED warehouse label-printer test that measured nothing about buyers or installers, so I do not cite it. Even read as real, it bears on no part of T2. T2 is kept, still uncertain, because the owner self-fitting observation pulls against installer control. New claim: none. Evidence: iims-boat-owner-diy.

T1 kept: SYN-D is a SIMULATED warehouse label-printer test that measured nothing about owners or buyers. Read as real, it would bear on no part of T1 and changes nothing. T1 stays unlikely on the real evidence: the price-gap observation pulls against a recognition premium. New claim: none. Evidence: rvdaily-owners-tempted.

T2 kept: What-if only: if SYN-D were real, it would be a warehouse label-printer test about packing errors. It says nothing about installers, owners or purchase channel, so it would change nothing for T2. This is a SIMULATED result and is not cited as evidence. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not build a direct consumer proposition now. Keep the core business as a B2B supplier to OEMs and specialist dealers. If leadership wants to test the consumer case, run the proposed installer-channel and branded price test (about EUR 18,000, 10 weeks, a proposed design that has not been run) before any product or channel investment. The evidence I could find is thin and mostly from company statements and anecdotal sources. Target customer: Not chosen. Candidates are owners of campers, vans and caravans who already fit or buy aftermarket heaters, reached through installers and accessory retailers. The evidence does not yet show which of these buyers matter.. Value proposition: Not established. A recognised-brand retrofit kit is a hypothesis. The evidence points to price sensitivity (owners are tempted by cheaper units) and to some owners fitting heaters themselves, so a premium brand promise is not yet supported.. Favoured theory: T2. Next action: Decide whether to fund the proposed installer-channel and branded price test (about EUR 18,000, 10 weeks, proposed). Before funding, ask the company for its own aftermarket and installer sales data, which is not public, and check whether it already sells through any consumer or accessory channel.. Uncertainty: High. Not public: Eberspaecher's aftermarket and consumer sales, installer and dealer contracts, margins, and whether it already sells direct to owners. The sources are a company trade-fair remark, a 2015 EU cartel finding about supplier concentration (old, EEA-wide, about market structure not channels), an Australian consumer article, a 2021 UK marine warning about boats, and a 2026 company press release on Asian competition. None measures purchase channel or willingness to pay for a branded consumer heater. The simulated result SYN-D was used only as a what-if and changes nothing.. Would change if: Company data shows a large share of aftermarket heater sales already goes direct to owners through its own channels, which would weaken T2 and favour a direct proposition; The branded test keeps at least 30 percent unit share at a +10 percent price premium, with at least half of sales reachable without installers, which would support a direct aftermarket proposition; Installers control more than 80 percent of sales and branded share falls below 15 percent at +10 percent, which would confirm a B2B or installer-supply posture; Credible evidence that owners pay a premium for recognised brands over cheap units, which would revive T1; Public evidence of Asian low-cost entry in the European aftermarket, which would make a consumer price fight less attractive. Beliefs: T1: unlikely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 72 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. Sample: 300 DIY woodworkers recruited via panel, balanced for age and gender. Target those who have used a CNC router for personal projects.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and willingness‑to‑pay (EUR). Secondary: self‑reported importance of precision vs. community features.. Decision rule: If Precision Pro’s purchase intent ≥ 45% and Community Connect’s ≤ 35%, conclude T1 is more likely. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Randomly assign participants to one of two message conditions: Condition A emphasizes safety and precision reduction gear certification for smart kitchen appliances; Condition B emphasizes safety and precision reduction gear certification for home rehabilitation devices (medical use). Both conditions include a willingness-to-pay price point and a purchase intent question.. Sample: 400 homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced across the two message conditions.. Measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of participants indicating they would purchase the product) and average willingness-to-pay price (in euros).. Predictions: T1: Condition A will show a higher purchase intent rate and higher willingness-to-pay price than Condition B.; T2: Condition B will show a higher purchase intent rate and higher willingness-to-pay price than Condition A.. Decision rule: If Condition A purchase intent rate ≥ 30% and Condition B purchase intent rate ≤ 20%, proceed to develop a consumer proposition for home automation (supporting T1). If Condition B purchase intent rate ≥ 30% and Condition A purchase intent rate ≤ 20%, proceed to develop a consumer proposition for home rehabilitation (supporting T2). If neither condition meets its threshold, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Constraints: Outside analysis from public sources only; company intentions are unknown; Financial and contractual detail may not be public; Test budget of 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Search budget is 8 in total, with 7 remaining; First establish what the company already sells to individual buyers; Brand and engineering credibility with industrial buyers must not be damaged. Alternatives: No expansion: keep the B2B machinery and plant focus and invest only in existing channels; Product redesign: adapt existing OELFLEX cables or connectors for a consumer use case such as DIY, home electronics, home EV charging, e-bike or smart-home wiring; Different route to buyers: sell existing products to individual buyers through online retail, electrical wholesalers or DIY chains, with no new product design; Different customer group: serve a consumer-adjacent segment such as electricians, installers or prosumers rather than end consumers; Service or bundled proposition: pre-assembled custom cable kits or configurators for makers and small installers; Adjacent B2B-to-consumer niche: EV charging or home energy cabling where the purchase is driven by installers.
Searched for "Lapp consumer online shop private customers"; found lapp-ev-accessory-competition, lapp-sales-network, lapp-mobility-private-checkout.

T1: Private buyers of EV home-charging accessories choose on price and convenience, so a manufacturer that already runs a direct-to-consumer shop can capture margin by selling its existing charging cables and accessories to owners without a new product. Who benefits: Private EV owners who want a simple purchase, and U.I. Lapp via its existing Lapp Mobility shop, which already serves private customers in Germany and Austria.. Why behaviour changes: Owners who buy a wallbox or cable themselves want a quick, clear online purchase. Direct checkout removes the intermediary's markup and makes the brand visible to the buyer, which can change which cable they buy.. How value is captured: Direct online sales margin on existing products through the existing shop, with no new product design and little added channel cost.. Assumptions: Private shop traffic for EV accessories is large enough to matter; Owners compare price online and are price-sensitive; The existing shop can convert visitors without a new product or new partner. Predictions: Private shop revenue for EV accessories rises when prices are cut to near competitor levels; Conversion is higher on product pages with clear fitting guidance than on price-only pages; Revenue stays small relative to B2B sales unless an installer channel is added.

T2: Private buyers do not choose cable or accessory brands themselves. An electrician or installer specifies the charging hardware, so the consumer-facing route only works if it runs through trade channels, and value is captured by winning installer trust and specification. Who benefits: Electricians and installers, who need a reliable, certified component that avoids callbacks, and U.I. Lapp, which already sells industrial cable and connection products to trade customers.. Why behaviour changes: Installers carry the liability for an installation and recommend products they trust and can get quickly. A brand trusted in industrial settings can transfer that trust to a trade-facing charging product, so the owner accepts the installer's choice.. How value is captured: Sales through electrical wholesalers and installer accounts, using existing trade relationships and certification, rather than direct consumer marketing.. Assumptions: Owners rarely specify cable or charging components themselves; Installers have a role in choosing EV charging components; Trade trust in the Lapp brand carries over to consumer-facing EV products. Predictions: Sales growth comes from installer and wholesaler accounts rather than shop traffic; Installers ask for certification and fast availability more than low price; Direct shop sales stay a small share of EV accessory revenue.

T1 supports, from lapp-mobility-private-checkout (company_assertion): "Als Privatkunde können Sie in unserem Shop mit folgenden Zahlungsarten bezahlen:". Does not show: Whether the shop makes any sales, how much revenue it earns, whether it sells EV accessories, or whether private shoppers buy in volume. The excerpt is cut off before the payment list, and the page is the company's own claim..

T2 neutral, from lapp-ev-accessory-competition (market_fact): "This reduces attractiveness for consumers, particularly in price-sensitive markets.". Does not show: Who specifies or buys EV charging hardware in practice, whether installers choose the brand, or whether installers would carry a Lapp consumer product. The article describes consumer price sensitivity, which does not decide between T1 and T2..

Looked for evidence against T1: "private EV charging accessories direct consumer online sales price competition installers"; found lapp-ev-accessory-competition, lapp-applications-channels, lapp-mobility-private-drivers.

T1 supports, from lapp-mobility-private-drivers (market_fact): "now offers products for electric car manufacturers, private electric car drivers, charging station manufacturers, infrastructure operators, and other companies active in the e-mobility sector.". Does not show: Any sales volume, share of revenue, or whether private drivers buy these products. An offering is not demand. The article does not show how many private drivers buy or whether they prefer buying direct..

Test "Two-channel pilot for EV home-charging accessories" between T1; T2. Method: Run a 10-week pilot of existing Lapp Mobility EV charging cables and accessories through two channels in parallel: (a) the existing private shop with a fitting-guidance page and a price matched to a competitor (proposed), and (b) a trade offer to 20 electrical wholesaler or installer accounts with the same product, plus a certification and fast-delivery pack (proposed). Track orders and inquiries in each channel. Use a fixed budget for paid traffic to the shop.. Sample: Shop: paid and organic traffic for the product pages, proposed at roughly 5,000 visits. Trade: 20 installer or wholesaler accounts in Germany (proposed), chosen from existing trade customers where possible.. Measure: Orders per 1,000 visits in the shop, and orders per active installer account in trade, over 10 weeks. Also the share of shop buyers who state they were advised by an electrician.. Predictions: T1: Shop orders per 1,000 visits are high enough to match or beat the trade channel's order value per account, and buyers do not mention an installer.; T2: Shop orders stay low and buyers mention an electrician; trade accounts order more value than the shop.. Decision rule: Proposed threshold: if shop orders reach at least 15 per 1,000 visits and at least 30% of shop buyers report no installer involvement, continue the direct shop route (T1). If trade accounts generate at least 2 times the order value per account of the shop, and at least 30% of shop buyers report installer involvement, prioritise the installer channel (T2). If neither threshold is met, do not invest beyond the pilot.. Cost: 20000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not build a new consumer product. Run the proposed two-channel pilot with existing EV charging products before any investment, since the evidence that private buyers are served is only company and trade-press assertion and demand is unmeasured. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: I keep T1 as a hypothesis. The simulated result is not real data and I do not count it as evidence. It concerns how a compatibility assurance changes purchase, which does not decide whether private buyers buy direct or through installers. Even read as a what-if, its added check resembles installer-style assurance, which points toward T2 rather than T1. The real evidence I cite is unchanged: a company claim of a private shop and a trade-press note on private driver offerings, neither of which shows demand. New claim: none. Evidence: lapp-mobility-private-checkout; lapp-mobility-private-drivers.

T2 kept: The simulated result, which I do not count as evidence, bears most on T2's mechanism: buyers respond to an assurance that the set will work, which fits trade-style trust better than self-checking. If it were real, it would favour installer-led assurance somewhat. But it was a recruited, hypothetical group and says nothing about whether installers would carry a consumer product. T2 stays uncertain, with no real evidence yet in its favour. New claim: none. Evidence: lapp-ev-accessory-competition.

T2 kept: Treated as a what-if only: SIMULATED, not real data, and not counted in any recommendation. If it were real, it would bear on T2's mechanism. Buyers chose the offer that promised a written assurance that the set would work, which fits trade-style trust, a modest point for T2. The recruited group and hypothetical setup leave the question open. T2 stays uncertain. The recommendation does not change. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-LAPP-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a new consumer product yet. U.I. Lapp already sells to private buyers through the Lapp Mobility shop in Germany and Austria, and trade press says it offers products to private EV drivers. Whether that yields demand is unknown. Run a small, reversible two-channel pilot with existing EV charging products (about EUR 20,000 over 10 weeks, proposed) and decide on the result. Target customer: Private EV owners buying home-charging cables and accessories (direct shop route), with electricians and wholesalers as a possible second route. The pilot tests which route carries the demand.. Value proposition: A clear, trusted purchase of existing certified cables and accessories, backed by industrial reliability. No new product design is proposed at this stage.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Set up the two-channel pilot: a private shop page with fitting guidance and a competitor-matched price, plus about 20 trade accounts. Record orders per 1,000 shop visits, orders per trade account, and whether shop buyers mention an installer. Apply the decision rule: at least 15 orders per 1,000 visits with at least 30% of buyers reporting no installer favours T1; trade accounts at least 2 times shop order value per account with at least 30% installer involvement favours T2. Also obtain internal shop revenue and EV accessory figures, which are not public.. Uncertainty: High. Shop sales volume, EV accessory revenue and margins are not public, and the shop page excerpt was cut off before its payment list. The trade-press sources describe the offering, not demand. T2 has no direct support in the sources I read. Competition is intense, with price-sensitive consumers. The test figures (sample, threshold, budget, weeks) are my estimates, not company data. A simulated result was read but is not counted as evidence.. Would change if: Internal shop data show EV accessory sales are negligible or unprofitable, which would favour no expansion; Pilot shop orders fall below 15 per 1,000 visits, or trade accounts order at least twice the shop value per account, which would shift weight toward T2 or no expansion; Evidence that electricians or wholesalers in practice choose the brand for owners, which would favour an installer-led route; Evidence that a consumer product would dilute the industrial brand with B2B customers; Real customer data showing owners buy on price alone with no installer involvement, which would strengthen T1. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

case.question: Should Nabtesco Corporation develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing precision reduction gears, automatic doors, transport equipment and welfare components sold to manufacturers, building owners and transport operators? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

The development in the 2025 financial year has once again shown that the close integration of the two product categories Products & Components (B2B) and Patient Care (B2C) as an integrated platform is paying off. The Patient Care business grew by 8.3 percent (organic growth: 4.9 percent), while the Products & Components business grew by as much as 14.5 percent (organic growth: 15.2 percent).

Nabtesco became the first in the world to develop a microprocessor-controlled intelligent prosthetic knee joint as mobility support equipment. The microprocessor detects the user’s walking speed, adjusts the pneumatic cylinder, and automatically controls the swing speed of the knee joint to help the person walk comfortably and naturally.

Thanks to their high reliability, Nabtesco’s precision reduction gears are preferred by a range of domestic and overseas robot manufacturers in the joints of their industrial robots, giving us a large share of the market. We have an approximately 60% (Nabtesco’s estimate) share of the global market for precision reduction gears when it comes to the joints of medium-size to large industrial robots.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Nabtesco should build a differentiated consumer-facing proposition for a specific individual-buyer use case, and what evidence would justify that investment, given its current B2B portfolio of reduction gears, automatic doors, transport components and welfare parts.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no company contact or intentions assumed; Company financial and contractual detail may be non-public; state the gaps; Test budget of 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; 8 searches in total (7 remaining), so evidence gathering must be targeted; Must first establish how far Nabtesco already reaches individual buyers, for example through prosthetics, door products or consumer-facing channels. Alternatives: No expansion: remain a B2B component supplier to robot makers, building owners and transport operators; Product redesign: adapt existing welfare components such as prosthetic knee joints for individual users through a direct or clinic-led offer; Different route to buyers: sell the same product to individuals through prosthetists, clinics or online channels; Different customer group: supply reduction gears and actuators to consumer robotics or personal mobility makers (B2B2C); Consumer-adjacent building products: residential automatic doors or home access products sold via installers or retailers to homeowners; Platform or service model: maintenance, monitoring or subscription services for the installed base of doors and gears.
Searched for "Nabtesco prosthetic knee joint individual patients sales"; found nabtesco-prosthetic-knee, nabtesco-reducer-share, nabtesco-ottobock-b2c.

T1: Individual buyers of Nabtesco's intelligent prosthetic knee would pay a premium for it only when a prosthetist or clinic recommends and fits it, so the value is captured through the clinical channel rather than direct consumer sales. Who benefits: Lower-limb amputees and their prosthetists, who need a fitted, adjustable device; Nabtesco, which would capture margin on a premium component sold through clinics.. Why behaviour changes: Users buy a prosthetic knee because a clinician prescribes and tunes it, and funding (insurance or public health) decides what they can access. Going direct to consumers removes the fitting and reimbursement that make the device usable.. How value is captured: Nabtesco sells components or systems to prosthetic makers and clinics, earning a premium on the microprocessor knee; the consumer price is set by the clinic and funder, not by Nabtesco.. Assumptions: Prosthetic knee purchases are mediated by clinicians and payers; Patients value the microprocessor knee enough to pay a premium when a clinic recommends it; Nabtesco's welfare line already sells through orthopaedic channels. Predictions: Clinics account for most fittings; direct-to-patient sales would be near zero without a clinician; Adoption varies with reimbursement rules across countries; A direct online offer would convert few buyers without fitting support.

T2: Individual buyers want a home-scale, self-installed access or mobility product, so a consumer offer would be captured by sales through retailers or installers to homeowners rather than by Nabtesco's current building and transport customers. Who benefits: Homeowners and older or disabled residents who want easier access; retailers and installers who would sell and fit the product; Nabtesco, if it could sell a compact, lower-cost door or actuator to these buyers.. Why behaviour changes: Homeowners buy when the product is cheap enough, simple to install and sold where they already shop. Current automatic doors are priced and specified for commercial buildings, so consumers do not see them as an option.. How value is captured: Nabtesco sells a redesigned, lower-cost unit through installer or retail channels, earning margin on a product line it does not yet sell to households.. Assumptions: Homeowners would pay for an automatic door or access product if the price and installation fit a home; Retail or installer channels can reach these buyers at acceptable cost; Commercial door know-how transfers to a smaller residential product. Predictions: Demand concentrates among buyers with accessibility needs rather than general consumers; Installer margins would decide adoption more than end-user price; A residential product would need a different price point than the commercial range.

T1 neutral, from nabtesco-prosthetic-knee (company_assertion): "Nabtesco became the first in the world to develop a microprocessor-controlled intelligent prosthetic knee joint as mobility support equipment.". Does not show: Who buys the knee, whether clinicians or payers mediate the sale, what it costs, or how many units are sold. It is the company's own description of a product, so it does not show demand or the sales channel..

T2 neutral, from nabtesco-reducer-share (company_assertion): "Thanks to their high reliability, Nabtesco’s precision reduction gears are preferred by a range of domestic and overseas robot manufacturers in the joints of their industrial robots, giving us a large share of the market.". Does not show: Anything about automatic doors, home access or residential buyers. It describes industrial robot gears sold to manufacturers, so it neither supports nor contradicts T2. The 60% share is the company's own estimate..
Looked for evidence against T1: "prosthetic knee direct-to-patient online purchase without prosthetist fitting"; found nabtesco-prosthetic-knee, nabtesco-ottobock-b2c.

Test "Channel-and-demand interview and landing-page test" between T1; T2. Method: Structured interviews with prosthetists, lower-limb amputees and home-access installers, plus a landing-page test offering two routes: clinic-referred and direct-to-consumer enquiry for a prosthetic knee, and an installer-referred enquiry for a residential automatic door or access product. Measure where buyers say they would buy and what price they would accept.. Sample: Proposed: 15 prosthetists, 40 lower-limb amputees recruited through clinics and patient groups, 15 residential installers or retailers, and a landing page open for 6 weeks.. Measure: Share of enquiries that route through a clinician or installer versus direct; stated willingness to pay; share of amputees who say they could be fitted without a prosthetist; installer margin requirement.. Predictions: T1: Most knee enquiries route through a prosthetist or clinic; few amputees say they could be fitted without one; direct enquiries convert poorly.; T2: Residential access enquiries come mainly from homeowners directly, with installers as a secondary route; a price point well below commercial door pricing draws most interest.. Decision rule: Proceed to a prototype only if at least 60% of knee enquiries and conversions route through clinics and stated willingness to pay supports a premium; if direct routes exceed 50% of qualified enquiries for residential access products at a price near the proposed level, consider the consumer route for T2. Otherwise do not expand. The 60% and 50% thresholds are proposed, not evidence-based.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not build a consumer-facing proposition on the evidence so far. If anything is pursued, it should be a clinic-led test around the intelligent prosthetic knee, not a direct-to-consumer launch. The public sources I could read show that Nabtesco makes a welfare product and a B2B gear and door business, but none show individual buyers, sales channels, prices or volumes. Our challenge search found no source contradicting T1, but it also found no direct evidence for it. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: unlikely.

T2 kept: SYN-NABTESCO-UPDATE is a SIMULATED what-if, not real data, so it cannot count as evidence. Taken as a what-if, it would point weakly against T2's assumption that a safety-framed home door offer draws buyers: the specification-only offer produced more deposits (72) than the safety-assurance offer (32) in the hypothetical arm. Even so, it tests one narrow mechanism in a recruited group, does not test installer margins or price, and does not change my belief that T2 is unsupported by any real source I have read. T2 stays kept but remains unsupported. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-NABTESCO-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Do not build a consumer-facing proposition now. Nabtesco already sells an intelligent prosthetic knee as welfare equipment, and the only route I can justify testing is clinic-led, not a direct-to-consumer launch. The public evidence does not show individual buyers, sales channels, prices or volumes for the welfare line, so I cannot recommend investment in a consumer offer. The residential door idea (T2) has no supporting source. Target customer: Lower-limb amputees fitted through prosthetists and clinics, and the prosthetists themselves. Residential access buyers are not a supported target.. Value proposition: A microprocessor-controlled prosthetic knee that adjusts swing speed to walking speed, sold through the clinical channel that fits and funds it. The benefit ('walk comfortably and naturally') is the company's own claim, not a validated result.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Do not start a launch. Gather Nabtesco's welfare channel and volume data first. Only if those show existing knee sales reach patients through clinics, run the proposed clinic-led test (X1, about 18000 EUR over 10 weeks; all figures proposed estimates).. Uncertainty: Large. Welfare sales, channel mix, pricing, reimbursement exposure and patient volumes were not found. The 60% gear share is the company's estimate. Ottobock's Patient Care B2C growth (8.3%, organic 4.9%) is a competitor figure and does not show Nabtesco's channel. My contrary-evidence search returned only the same two sources, so the absence of contradiction is weak.. Would change if: Nabtesco welfare data show a meaningful share of knee sales already reaches patients directly without a clinician or payer; Interviews show amputees can be fitted without a prosthetist and would buy online near the proposed price; A real test shows residential access buyers, via installers or retailers, convert well enough to support installer margins (T2); Reimbursement rules make a premium knee unfundable, which would sink the clinic route. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: unlikely.

case.question: Should Rieter Holding AG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing short-staple spinning machines, components and after-sales services for industrial spinning mills? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: Over the last few years, the spinning industry has continued to move to Asia. As a consequence, Rieter, the leading supplier of systems for short-staple fibre spinning, has made significant investments in China and India adding production capacities in these countries.
The world market for staple fiber machines relevant to Rieter has an annual volume of CHF 2 200 million to CHF 4 000 million. Rieter is the market leader with a share of about 30 percent.

Owing to extraordinary restructuring expenses and transaction costs in connection with the acquisition of Barmag in the amount of CHF 54.2 million, Rieter closed the 2025 financial year with a net loss of CHF 63.4 million (2024: net profit of CHF 10.4 million).

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Rieter Holding AG should develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its existing offerings in short-staple spinning machines, components, and after-sales services for industrial spinning mills.. Constraints: Budget of 20,000 euros and 12-week test period.; Publicly available information only, with potential limitations in accessing financial and contractual details.; Company has not explicitly stated its intentions or been contacted for this analysis.. Alternatives: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case.; Redesign existing products.; Pursue a different route to buyers (e.g., direct-to-consumer sales).; Target a different customer group.; No expansion (maintain current market focus).; Other (specify).

Searched for "individual buyers Rieter Holding AG current market reach; Rieter Holding AG Barmag integration impact; short-staple spin"; found rieter-industry-in-asia, rieter-market-share, rieter-net-loss-2025.

T1: Rieter Holding AG can tap into a growing market for premium, specialized spinning solutions by developing a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, such as sustainable or high-performance fibers. This shift could attract new customers beyond its traditional industrial spinning mill clients. Who benefits: Rieter Holding AG. Why behaviour changes: By offering unique, specialized spinning solutions, Rieter can appeal to a broader range of customers who value performance, sustainability, or other specific attributes. This could lead to increased market share and higher profit margins.. How value is captured: By differentiating its products and services, Rieter can command premium prices and attract customers willing to pay for specialized solutions. This could be achieved through innovative design, superior quality, or tailored support services. Assumptions: The market for specialized spinning solutions is growing.; Rieter has the technical expertise and resources to develop these solutions.; There is a demand for products focused on sustainability or high-performance fibers.. Predictions: Increased market share in the specialized spinning segment.; Higher average selling prices for new products.; Expansion into new geographic markets or customer segments..

T2: Rieter Holding AG could capitalize on the growing demand for sustainable and eco-friendly textiles by introducing a line of spinning machines and services tailored to produce these fibers. This move would allow them to differentiate themselves from competitors by positioning themselves as a leader in sustainable spinning solutions. Who benefits: Rieter Holding AG. Why behaviour changes: Consumers and businesses are increasingly demanding sustainable and eco-friendly products. By offering specialized spinning solutions for sustainable fibers, Rieter can attract environmentally conscious customers and command a premium price. How value is captured: Rieter can capture value by: 1) offering exclusive designs and technologies for sustainable spinning, 2) providing expert consultation on sustainable fiber production, and 3) building a strong brand image as a leader in eco-friendly textile. Assumptions: The market for sustainable textiles is expanding.; Rieter has the technical knowledge and resources to develop sustainable spinning solutions.; There is a willingness among customers to pay a premium for eco-friendly products.. Predictions: Increased market share in the sustainable textiles segment.; Higher average selling prices for sustainable spinning machines and services.; Establishment of Rieter as a leader in sustainable textile production..

T3: Rieter Holding AG can capitalize on the growing demand for sustainable textiles by introducing a line of spinning machines and services tailored to produce these fibers. This move would position them as a leader in sustainable spinning solutions, attracting environmentally conscious customers and allowing them to command a premium price. Who benefits: Rieter Holding AG. Why behaviour changes: Consumers and businesses are increasingly demanding sustainable and eco-friendly products. By offering specialized spinning solutions for sustainable fibers, Rieter can tap into this growing market and differentiate itself from competitors.. How value is captured: Rieter can capture value by: 1) offering exclusive designs and technologies for sustainable spinning, 2) providing expert consultation on sustainable fiber production, and 3) building a strong brand image as a leader in eco-friendly textile. Assumptions: The market for sustainable textiles is expanding.; Rieter has the technical knowledge and resources to develop sustainable spinning solutions.; There is a willingness among customers to pay a premium for eco-friendly products.. Predictions: Increased market share in the sustainable textiles segment.; Higher average selling prices for sustainable spinning machines and services.; Establishment of Rieter as a leader in sustainable textile production..

T3 supports, from rieter-industry-in-asia (company_assertion): "Over the last few years, the spinning industry has continued to move to Asia.". Does not show: The exact extent of Rieter's current market reach among individual buyers, or their plans for future expansion into new markets..

T3 neutral, from rieter-net-loss-2025 (company_assertion): "Owing to extraordinary restructuring expenses and transaction costs in connection with the acquisition of Barmag in the amount of CHF 54.2 million, Rieter closed the 2025 financial year with a net loss of CHF 63.4 million (2024: net profit of CHF 10.4 million).". Does not show: The exact reasons for the 2025 net loss, or the impact of the Barmag acquisition on Rieter's future financial performance..

T3 supports, from rieter-market-share (company_assertion): "The world market for staple fiber machines relevant to Rieter has an annual volume of CHF 2 200 million to CHF 4 000 million.". Does not show: The exact market share of Rieter, or the size of its customer base among individual buyers..

T1 supports, from rieter-industry-in-asia (company_assertion): "Over the last few years, the spinning industry has continued to move to Asia.". Does not show: The exact extent of Rieter's current market reach among individual buyers, or their plans for future expansion into new markets..

T2 supports, from rieter-industry-in-asia (company_assertion): "Over the last few years, the spinning industry has continued to move to Asia.". Does not show: The exact extent of Rieter's current market reach among individual buyers, or their plans for future expansion into new markets..

Looked for evidence against T3: "Is there evidence that Rieter Holding AG is already actively pursuing a strategy to capitalize on the growing demand for"; found rieter-customers-3000, rieter-com4recycling-license, rieter-industry-in-asia.

Test "Market Viability Test: Differentiated Spinning Solutions" between T1; T2; T3. Method: Mixed-methods: Online survey and in-depth case studies. Sample: 150 individual buyers: 75 current customers (industrial spinning mills) and 75 potential new customers (textile manufacturers with focus on performance, sustainability, or niche applications). Measure: Willingness to pay a premium for differentiated spinning solutions; current use of specialized fibers; interest in switching to Rieter's offerings; perceived value of sustainability, performance, or niche features.. Predictions: T1: New customers (non-spinning mill) will show higher willingness to pay and interest in Rieter's differentiated solutions.; T2: All respondents, regardless of customer type, will express high interest and willingness to pay for sustainable spinning solutions.; T3: A mix of high and low interest/willingness to pay, reflecting current market adoption levels for specialized fibers.. Decision rule: If the average willingness to pay for differentiated/sustainable solutions exceeds CHF 4000, the test predicts market viability for the proposed strategy.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.
The investigation stopped before a recommendation (repeated errors).

case.question: Should U.I. Lapp GmbH develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing cables and connection technology for industrial machinery and plant engineering? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify U.I. Lapp GmbH investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial cable and connector offerings.. T1: Consumers will adopt LAPP products for a specific use case (e.g., home networking, outdoor recreation, automotive aftermarket) if they perceive the product as a premium, reliable solution that offers superior performance or safety compared to generic alternatives. Who benefits: Consumers seeking high-quality, durable connections for their home, outdoor, or automotive needs.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers learn that LAPP products are engineered for industrial reliability and offer features such as weatherproofing, durability, or safety certifications, they will be willing to pay a premium price for them.. How value is captured: U.I. Lapp GmbH can capture value by pricing the differentiated consumer products at a premium, selling them through retail or direct-to-consumer channels, and leveraging its brand reputation for industrial quality.. Assumptions: Consumers are aware of LAPP's industrial reputation and are willing to research it.; There is a measurable willingness to pay for premium features in consumer products.; Retail or online channels can effectively reach the target consumer segment.. Predictions: In a test offering a premium-priced consumer product, purchase intent or actual purchases will be higher than for a lower-priced generic alternative.; Surveyed consumers will cite industrial reliability, durability, or safety as primary reasons for choosing the product..

T2: Consumers will adopt LAPP products for a specific use case (e.g., home networking, outdoor recreation, automotive aftermarket) if they perceive the product as a convenient, plug-and-play solution that integrates easily into their existing setup, reducing installation complexity. Who benefits: Consumers who value ease of use and quick deployment for their home, outdoor, or automotive needs.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers learn that LAPP products offer pre-wired, easy-to-connect connectors or accessories that eliminate the need for manual wiring or complex assembly, they will be willing to purchase them as a time-saving convenience.. How value is captured: U.I. Lapp GmbH can capture value by offering bundled, pre-assembled consumer kits at a premium, selling them through retail or online channels, and leveraging its existing distribution network to reach consumers.. Assumptions: Consumers prioritize convenience and quick installation over cost.; There is a measurable willingness to pay for pre-assembled, plug-and-play products.; Retail or online channels can effectively promote and sell these convenience-focused products.. Predictions: In a test offering a convenience-focused consumer product, purchase intent or actual purchases will be higher than for a lower-priced generic alternative.; Surveyed consumers will cite ease of installation and quick setup as primary reasons for choosing the product..

Test "Consumer Product Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product offers and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and geographic regions to reflect a broad consumer base.. Measure: 1) Purchase intent: binary (would buy) or WTP (maximum price willing to pay). 2) Primary reason for choosing the product (open-ended).. Predictions: T1: Consumers will indicate purchase intent or WTP for a premium-priced LAPP product at least 20% higher than for a lower-priced generic alternative, and will cite industrial reliability, durability, or safety as the primary reason.; T2: Consumers will indicate purchase intent or WTP for a convenience-focused LAPP product at least 20% higher than for a lower-priced generic alternative, and will cite ease of installation and quick setup as the primary reason.. Decision rule: If the premium-priced product's purchase intent or WTP exceeds the convenience-focused product's by at least 20 percentage points, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the premium-priced product's purchase intent or WTP is not at least 20 points higher, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition. If both products show similar performance, conduct further market research.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows LAPP products are used in industrial applications and are already sold to consumers in electromobility, but it does not demonstrate consumer willingness to pay a premium for industrial reliability or that convenience is a primary driver. Conduct the proposed Consumer Product Preference Test to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated result (SYN-LAPP-UPDATE) does not address T1, as it tests compatibility uncertainty, not premium-priced product demand. Therefore T1 remains unchanged. case.question: Should Sika AG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing construction chemicals, sealants and adhesives for contractors, distributors and industrial manufacturers? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the application-kit offer and 32 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "DIY Messaging Test: Professional vs Convenience Framing" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners who have completed a home improvement project in the past year. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: Professional Condition (highlighting professional-grade performance, reliability, and use by contractors) or Convenience Condition (highlighting easy application, minimal skill required, and time savings). After viewing the product description, participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and whether they would pay a premium over a generic alternative.. Sample: Proposed sample: 1,200 homeowners (600 per condition) from a panel, balanced for age, gender, and home improvement experience. Recruitment cost: €2,000.. Measure: Primary measure: average purchase intent score (Professional Condition vs Convenience Condition). Secondary measure: premium willingness to pay (difference in price premium indicated).. Predictions: T1: Professional Condition will yield higher average purchase intent and premium willingness to pay than Convenience Condition.; T2: Convenience Condition will yield higher average purchase intent and premium willingness to pay than Professional Condition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for Professional Condition is at least 1.5 points higher than for Convenience Condition (i.e., Professional ≥ 5.5 and Convenience ≤ 4.0), conclude T1 is supported. If the difference is ≤ 1.5 points, conclude neither theory is supported. If neither condition meets the threshold, the test is inconclusive and further research is needed.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

case.question: Should Kardex Holding AG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing automated storage and retrieval systems (vertical lift modules, carousels and AutoStore-based systems) for warehouses, factories and organisations? What evidence would justify that investment?

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. In this simulated warehouse test, a new label printer reduced packing errors slightly. Nothing about wearers or buyers was measured.

Kardex automated storage systems bring speed, structure, and visibility to dealership parts departments. They condense storage footprints, increase on-hand inventory, and allow service operations to run more efficiently—resulting in faster repairs, higher throughput, and increased customer satisfaction.
Kardex has been a significant name in business data storage since 1898, tracing back to the Rand Ledger Company.

Kardex pre-owned systems deliver the same space-saving, efficiency-boosting performance you'd expect from our solutions and at a fraction of the cost and lead time. Whether you're scaling up, replacing legacy equipment, or taking your first step into automated storage, a pre-owned Kardex system gets you there faster.

events.text: Objective: Find out whether Kardex Holding AG should invest in a differentiated consumer-facing proposition for a specific use case beyond its warehouse and factory storage systems, and what evidence would justify that investment. The real question is where a maker of automated storage hardware could capture value in a buyer segment it does not serve well today.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; the company has not asked this question and has not been contacted; Financial and contractual detail such as AutoStore partnership terms may not be public; Test budget of EUR 20,000 and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Search budget: 7 searches remaining; Company intentions must not be presented as fact; claims must come from sources I have read. Alternatives: No expansion: stay B2B industrial and warehouse focused and optimise the existing AutoStore, vertical lift module and carousel channel; Modular product redesign sold through retailers, e-commerce or an online configurator to small buyers; Different customer group: small and medium businesses, workshops, pharmacies or healthcare storage, or small fulfilment operations; Storage as a service or partner-led: lease or install for households, or license a product through an existing consumer storage brand.
Searched for "Kardex consumer home storage"; found kardex-dealership-parts, kardex-filing-history, kardex-portfolio.

T1: Kardex's existing compact automated storage can be sold profitably to small-footprint commercial buyers, such as dealership parts counters and small service workshops, through its existing B2B sales channel, without any consumer offer. Who benefits: Small commercial operators with limited floor space and high parts or tool counts, and Kardex through repeat sales of existing hardware to a new buyer segment.. Why behaviour changes: A parts department that searches shelves by hand loses time and stock visibility. Compact automated storage that condenses footprint and shows stock levels reduces wait times, which the company says leads to faster repairs and higher throughput.. How value is captured: Kardex sells and services its own hardware and software to a segment reached through dealership groups or distributors, so it keeps the margin on hardware, installation and service without building a retail brand.. Assumptions: Dealership parts departments are a real, paying buyer segment for Kardex products; The company's marketing claims about dealership benefits reflect actual customer outcomes; Small-footprint variants can be sold at a price that small operators will pay back through labour and time savings; Distributor or dealer-group channels can reach these buyers without new consumer marketing. Predictions: Dealership or service-centre installations appear in Kardex customer references or case studies; Sales growth in small-footprint or dealership applications would be visible in customer count rather than average order value; Buyers would compare cost against parts-search time saved, with payback measured in months rather than years.

T2: Individual households will not buy automated storage at Kardex price points, because the value of automation depends on high throughput and volume that a home does not have. A consumer offer would only work as a rented or subscription service, not a sale. Who benefits: Households with large volumes of stored items, such as collectors or home-office owners, who would pay for convenience but not for capital equipment; the manufacturer would capture recurring rental fees instead of hardware margin.. Why behaviour changes: A household does not need fast retrieval of many items each day, so capital cost is hard to justify. Renting or subscribing spreads cost over time and removes the purchase decision, which may change behaviour where an outright sale would not.. How value is captured: Kardex would earn recurring fees on installed units and keep ownership of the hardware, which could fit a service model better than a one-off sale.. Assumptions: Household throughput is too low to justify automation on time savings alone; Consumers would accept a monthly fee over a purchase price; Installation and servicing costs for homes can be kept low enough to make rental viable. Predictions: Stated willingness to pay for home storage would be far below the hardware cost; Rental or subscription uptake would be higher than outright purchase uptake in any consumer trial; Demand would concentrate in households with high item counts and frequent retrieval, not general households.

T1 supports, from kardex-dealership-parts (company_assertion): "Kardex automated storage systems bring speed, structure, and visibility to dealership parts departments. They condense storage footprints, increase on-hand inventory, and allow service operations to run more efficiently". Does not show: It is the company's own marketing, so it does not show that any dealership has bought the product, what it paid, or whether the promised speed and inventory gains happened. It does not show that dealership parts departments are a meaningful revenue segment, and it says nothing about small operators outside the automotive sector..

T2 neutral, from kardex-portfolio (company_assertion): "Kardex provides an intelligent entry into automation with its dynamic storage and retrieval systems, offers integrated material handling systems, small parts storage systems including multi-shuttle technology, and automated high-bay warehouses.". Does not show: The profile lists only industrial and warehouse products. It says nothing about household demand, pricing, throughput of home users, or any rental or subscription model, so it neither supports nor rules out T2..
Looked for evidence against T1: "automated storage small business payback cost not justified"; found kardex-portfolio, kardex-pre-owned, kardex-filing-history.

T1 neutral, from kardex-pre-owned (company_assertion): "Whether you're scaling up, replacing legacy equipment, or taking your first step into automated storage, a pre-owned Kardex system gets you there faster.". Does not show: It is a sales claim for used equipment in the UK. It shows the company targets first-time and cost-sensitive buyers, which fits T1's small-operator buyer, but it gives no price, buyer type, or volume, and it does not show that small operators are a profitable segment. It is not a counter-example to T1..

Test "Small-operator versus household demand pilot" between T1; T2. Method: Offer two compact, illustrative product descriptions (not a built product) to two groups: small service businesses with parts or tool counts (dealership parts counters, independent workshops, small healthcare or pharmacy back rooms) and households with high item counts (collectors, home offices). Each respondent sees a purchase price and a monthly rental price, and is asked for a refundable deposit or letter of intent. Track conversion and the stated reason for declining.. Sample: Proposed: 40 small-business contacts and 60 household contacts, recruited through trade associations, workshop networks and online collector groups. Analyst estimate, not company data.. Measure: Share of contacts who give a deposit or signed letter of intent at the stated price, split by purchase and rental option, and the stated reason for declining.. Predictions: T1: Small-business deposit or letter-of-intent rate is clearly higher than household rate, and small businesses mention time saved on parts or item retrieval as the reason to buy.; T2: Household rate is similar to or higher than the small-business rate on a rental basis, and rental is preferred to purchase; small-business rate is low because price, not use case, is the barrier.. Decision rule: Proposed threshold: if at least 10% of small-business contacts give a deposit or letter of intent and this is at least twice the household rate, keep T1 and scope a small-footprint B2B variant. If household rental uptake is at least 5% and above small-business uptake, consider a rental model for households and revisit T2. If neither group reaches 5%, reject both and do not invest.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not build a consumer proposition now. The evidence I found is company marketing only and shows Kardex sells to dealership parts departments and first-time buyers, which is consistent with a small-footprint B2B variant. Test that segment before any investment. Household demand is unproven and looks weak on price, so T2 stays open but is not the lead. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: SYN-D is a SIMULATED result about a label printer and packing errors. It measured nothing about buyers or small-footprint storage, so it does not bear on T1 and I do not cite it. T1 stays as it was: the only support I have read is company marketing for dealership parts departments, and the small-operator segment is untested. New claim: none. Evidence: kardex-dealership-parts.

T2 kept: Supposing SYN-D were real, it would still bear on neither theory. It is a SIMULATED label-printer result that measured nothing about households, rental, or buyers, so it changes nothing for T2. T2 stays untested: its only support is a cost argument, and the corporate profile I read is neutral on it. New claim: none. Evidence: kardex-portfolio.

T1 kept: Supposing SYN-D were real: a label printer reducing packing errors is a what-if about warehouse throughput, not about small-operator buyers, so it would not change T1. I do not count it as evidence for T1. T1 stays kept on the basis of company marketing alone, and the segment is still untested. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D; kardex-dealership-parts.

Recommendation: Do not build a consumer-facing proposition now. The evidence I could read shows Kardex sells automated storage to commercial buyers, including dealership parts departments, and markets pre-owned units as a first step for cost-sensitive buyers. I found no source showing Kardex sells to individual households. If the company wants to test a differentiated offer, the cheapest sensible step is a small-footprint B2B variant for small service operators, tested before any product work. Household demand looks unproven and price-constrained. Target customer: Small commercial operators with limited floor space and high parts or tool counts, such as dealership parts counters and small service workshops. Households are not supported by the evidence I read.. Value proposition: Compact automated storage that saves retrieval time and frees floor space, with stock visibility, offered as a lower-cost entry or pre-owned option. This is a hypothesis drawn from company marketing, not a validated proposition.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the small-operator versus household pilot (X1) as proposed, with about 40 small-business and 60 household contacts, a 12-week limit and a EUR 20,000 budget, all analyst estimates. Before running it, check whether Kardex has existing dealership or workshop customer data, which may be non-public, that would already show whether T1 holds.. Uncertainty: Large. I found no independent evidence of sales volume, customer outcomes, pricing or margins for any small-operator or consumer segment. The sources read were company marketing (dealership page, corporate profile, pre-owned page) plus a Wikipedia history excerpt that says nothing relevant. AutoStore partnership terms and consumer channel revenue are not public in what I could access. The budget, timeline, sample sizes and thresholds are my proposals, not company figures. T2 is untested and rests on a cost argument, not evidence.. Would change if: Kardex's own customer or sales data shows dealership or small-operator buyers are a small or unprofitable segment; Independent evidence shows small operators do not reach payback on compact automated storage within a reasonable period; The pilot shows household rental or subscription deposit uptake at or above 5% and above small-business uptake, which would revive T2; Evidence shows the pre-owned channel is mainly used by large buyers, which would weaken the entry-level argument for small operators; A non-company source documents actual dealership or workshop installations and their outcomes. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Test "Bag Drop Experiment" between T1; T2. Method: Randomized controlled trial (RCT) with a 2x2 design. T1: Consumers will adopt a consumer‑facing reverse vending machine (RVM) for residential deposit return if they perceive a convenient, digital refund mechanism that is easy to use and accessible via a mobile app, because convenience and digital payout reduce friction and increase willingness to return containers. Who benefits: Individual consumers who receive digital refunds and can return containers from home, and retailers who gain foot traffic and can brand themselves as eco‑friendly.. Why behaviour changes: Convenience (no need to visit a redemption center) and digital refund (instant payout without cash) lower perceived effort and reduce barriers to participation.. How value is captured: TOMRA can charge a subscription fee for the app and service, or earn revenue from data on consumer return habits that can be sold to retailers or recycling programs.. Assumptions: Consumers trust the app to accurately track returns and provide refunds.; Retailers are willing to partner with TOMRA to offer the service and promote it to customers.; Regulatory frameworks in target markets permit digital refund mechanisms for deposit return.. Predictions: In a test offering the app to a residential building, at least 30% of residents will register and return containers within the first month.; Surveyed satisfaction with the digital refund process will be rated “very satisfied” by at least 70% of users.; Retailers will report increased foot traffic and repeat purchases among customers who use the app for bottle returns..

T2: Consumers will adopt a consumer‑facing reverse vending machine (RVM) for residential deposit return if they receive a tangible cash refund (e.g., a voucher or coin return) that is easily redeemable at nearby retailers, because physical money provides immediate gratification and reduces trust concerns about digital refunds. Who benefits: Individual consumers who receive cash refunds and can redeem them for goods or services, and retailers who gain additional foot traffic and can partner to facilitate redemption.. Why behaviour changes: Physical cash eliminates the need for a digital refund mechanism and associated trust in app accuracy, making the return process more tangible and convenient for consumers.. How value is captured: TOMRA can charge a subscription fee for the cash‑return service, or earn revenue from retailer partnerships that share redemption revenue.. Assumptions: Consumers prefer physical cash refunds over digital refunds for deposit returns.; Retailers are willing to accept and redeem consumer‑generated RVM returns as a marketing incentive.; Regulatory frameworks permit cash refunds for consumer‑generated deposits.. Predictions: In a test offering cash refunds via a vending machine, at least 25% of participating households will redeem at least one refund within two weeks.; Surveyed satisfaction with cash refund will be rated “very satisfied” by at least 60% of users.; Retailers will report a measurable increase in purchases from customers who use the cash‑return service..

Test "Digital vs Cash Refund Consumer Pilot" between T1; T2. Method: Randomized controlled trial with two parallel groups in a residential building (e.g., apartment complex). Group A receives a digital refund via the myTOMRA app; Group B receives a tangible cash refund (e.g., voucher or coin return) via a vending machine. Both groups have access to the same sensor-based sorting bin and can return containers at any time. The test runs for 12 weeks, with weekly. Sample: 200 households (100 per group) in a building with a high density of residents who shop at nearby retailers.. Measure: 1) Number of containers returned per household per week (digital refund group vs cash refund group). 2) Self-reported satisfaction with refund process (digital vs cash) on a 1‑10 scale. 3) Retailer foot traffic data (if available) for stores located near the building.. Predictions: T1: Group A (digital refund) will have at least 30% higher return rates than Group B (cash refund) and higher satisfaction ratings, because convenience and digital payout reduce friction.; T2: Group B (cash refund) will have at least 30% higher return rates than Group A (digital refund) and higher satisfaction ratings, because physical cash provides immediate gratification and reduces trust concerns.. Decision rule: If Group A’s return rate exceeds Group B’s by at least 15 percentage points (e.g., 35% vs 20%) and Group A’s satisfaction score is at least 2 points higher than Group B’s, then T1 is supported. If Group B’s return rate exceeds Group A’s by at least 15 percentage points and Group B’s satisfaction score is at least 2 points higher, then T2 is supported. If neither. Cost: 18000 euros, 12 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
