Test "Hobbyist Willingness-to-Pay Survey" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are recruited from a panel of hobbyists and small-scale producers. They are shown a mock product description of a compact spinning machine (e.g., a mini card spinning machine) and asked to indicate their maximum price they would pay and the features they would accept. The survey also includes a willingness-to-pay question for a premium version with additional features.. Sample: Proposed sample: 300 participants (150 hobbyists and 150 small-scale producers) recruited via an online panel. Stratified by age, gender, and geographic region to ensure diversity.. Measure: Primary measure: average willingness-to-pay (WTP) for the compact spinning machine. Secondary measure: share of participants who would pay a premium over a baseline price of CHF 200.. Predictions: T1: Average WTP will be above CHF 200, and at least 30% of participants will indicate a premium price.; T2: Average WTP will be below CHF 200, and fewer than 20% of participants will indicate a premium price.. Decision rule: If average WTP is above CHF 200 and at least 30% indicate a premium price, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If average WTP is below CHF 200 and fewer than 20% indicate a premium price, do not invest in a consumer proposition. If the average WTP is between CHF 150 and CHF 200, conduct a follow-up survey to understand the reasons for the lower price sensitivity.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting hobbyists and small-scale producers, as supported by the Artisan line and the presence of a consumer webshop. However, validate demand through a willingness-to-pay survey before committing resources. If the survey shows average willingness-to-pay below CHF 200 and low premium pricing, reconsider the investment; otherwise, develop a compact spinning machine, Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting hobbyists and small-scale producers, as supported by the Artisan line and the presence of a consumer webshop. However, validate demand through a willingness-to-pay survey before committing resources. If the survey shows average willingness-to-pay below CHF 200 and low premium pricing, reconsider the investment; otherwise, develop a compact spinning machine, Target customer: Hobbyists and small-scale producers who currently lack access to compact, affordable spinning equipment.. Value proposition: An affordable, compact spinning machine that automates key steps and brings speed to the creative process, sold through Rieter’s existing webshop.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed 8‑week, €15,000 willingness-to-pay survey with 300 participants to measure price sensitivity and premium willingness. Use the decision rule to decide whether to proceed with development or abandon the consumer proposition.. Uncertainty: The actual size of the hobbyist market and Rieter’s ability to produce a profitable consumer product remain uncertain. Financial constraints (e.g., net loss in 2025) and the lack of public evidence on willingness to pay add to the ambiguity. Would change if: If the survey shows average willingness-to-pay below CHF 200 and fewer than 20% indicate a premium price, reconsider the investment.; If new evidence shows a large, growing market for home spinning or Rieter’s ability to achieve positive margins on a consumer product, the recommendation would shift toward developing the proposition.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

events.text: Objective: Decide whether U.I. Lapp GmbH should build a differentiated proposition for individual buyers beyond its industrial cable and connection business. First establish whether it already reaches individual buyers. Then identify a causal reason an individual would pay for a Lapp-made offer, and what evidence would justify the investment.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no contact with the company; the company has not asked this question; Financial and contractual detail may be non-public; state what could not be found; Test budget of EUR 20000 and a 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Search budget of 8 (7 left); read at least three sources before theorising; Any claim about current consumer sales must come from a source read; Do not cite SIMULATED results as evidence. Alternatives: No expansion: remain a B2B cable and connection supplier to machinery and plant engineering; Adjacent B2B expansion: sell existing products to food, logistics, energy and mobility OEMs; Product redesign for one use case sold through existing channels, such as EV charging cable assemblies; Direct consumer channel: branded online sales of cables and accessories to individuals; Partner route: license or co-brand with retailers or charging-station makers rather than running own retail; Customer switch to prosumers or small workshops, or sell a configurator or cable-assembly service to small buyers.
Searched for "Lapp consumer online shop cables individuals"; found lapp-ev-accessory-competition, lapp-mobility-private-checkout, lapp-wallbox-light-home.

T1: Private EV owners pay a premium for a home charging product from an established industrial cable maker because it signals electrical safety and reliability, so a Lapp-branded home wallbox or cable set sold through its own shop can earn a margin above generic alternatives. Who benefits: Private EV owners who want a safe, reliable home charging installation and a seller they trust; Lapp Mobility, which captures margin on the product and the shop channel.. Why behaviour changes: Owners worry about fire and installation risk in garages. A brand known for industrial-grade cables and connectors reduces that perceived risk, which justifies paying more than for a low-cost import.. How value is captured: Lapp Mobility sells the wallbox and accessories directly through its online shop to private customers, keeping the retail margin and selling add-ons and cable sets.. Assumptions: Buyers rate electrical safety and brand trust above unit price for home charging; The DIY installation claim (three screws) does not deter buyers who need an electrician; Lapp's industrial reputation transfers to the consumer product. Predictions: Lapp-branded wallbox sells at a price above comparable generic wallboxes in the same retailers; Buyers who cite safety or brand in reviews or surveys account for a large share of purchases; Conversion from shop visit to purchase is higher than for generic sellers with the same product.

T2: Private EV owners buy home charging on price and convenience, so a consumer-facing product from an industrial cable maker faces a commodity market with no premium. Value stays with B2B supply to OEMs and installers, not with individuals. Who benefits: Private EV owners, who gain low prices; installers and OEM buyers, who keep the volume; Lapp only if it stays in B2B supply.. Why behaviour changes: The source describes a fiercely contested, price-sensitive market where start-ups have been pushed out. When many sellers offer similar wallboxes, buyers compare price and do not pay for brand.. How value is captured: Lapp earns margin on components and assemblies sold to wallbox makers, installers and OEMs, and does not need its own consumer margin or shop.. Assumptions: Wallboxes are close substitutes, so brand carries little price premium; Consumer purchase is driven mainly by price and installation cost; Retail channel costs (marketing, returns, shipping) erode margin on low-ticket items. Predictions: Lapp-branded wallboxes price close to or below generic equivalents, with weak sales at a premium; Consumer sales volumes are small relative to B2B revenue; Buyers' stated reasons focus on price and availability, not brand or safety.

T2 supports, from lapp-ev-accessory-competition (market_fact): "This reduces attractiveness for consumers, particularly in price-sensitive markets.". Does not show: This is a trade article, not sales data. It does not give Lapp's consumer volumes, prices or margins, and it does not show what share of buyers choose on price rather than brand..

T1 neutral, from lapp-wallbox-light-home (company_assertion): "Die Montage können Sie in wenigen Minuten mit nur drei Schrauben selbst durchführen.". Does not show: This is the seller's product description (in German: you can fit it yourself in a few minutes with three screws). It says nothing about buyers' safety concerns, brand trust, willingness to pay a premium, or sales. It is a company claim, not proof of demand..
Looked for evidence against T2: "home wallbox buyers pay premium brand safety quality price"; found lapp-ev-accessory-competition, lapp-wago-smart-home, lapp-eon-home-charging.

T2 neutral, from lapp-eon-home-charging (company_assertion): "Laut einer repräsentativen Umfrage, die Civey im Auftrag von Eon durchgeführt hat, laden 63 Prozent ihr Auto am häufigsten zuhause.". Does not show: This survey was commissioned by E.ON, an energy company with an interest in home charging, and was run by Civey. It shows that 63 percent of German e-car drivers most often charge at home (in German: 63 percent most often charge their car at home). It does not show whether buyers choose on price or on brand, or whether they would pay a premium for a Lapp product. It supports that a home market exists, which both theories need..

Test "Brand premium test on a home wallbox listing" between T1; T2. Method: Run paid search and social ads for the same wallbox in two arms: one shows the Lapp brand and one shows a generic, unbranded listing, both at the same price. Then run a price step with the Lapp listing at about +10 percent versus the generic. Compare click-through, add-to-cart and purchase rates. Use the existing shop or a landing page with the same checkout (proposed design).. Sample: Proposed: about 8,000 ad-exposed German EV-owner or EV-interest users, roughly 4,000 per arm, over 6 weeks. Estimated sample size, not from a source.. Measure: Purchase conversion per exposed user and click-through rate, by arm. Also post-purchase reason survey (price, brand, safety, installation) on buyers.. Predictions: T1: Lapp-branded listing converts at the same or higher rate than the generic listing at equal price, and still converts at a +10 percent price with little drop. Buyers cite safety or brand as a reason.; T2: Brand makes no difference to conversion at equal price, and the +10 percent price cuts conversion clearly. Buyers cite price and availability.. Decision rule: Proposed threshold: keep T1 for a consumer offer only if the branded listing converts at least 20 percent more than the generic listing at equal price, and the +10 percent arm keeps at least 80 percent of the conversion of the equal-price branded arm. Otherwise reject T1 and do not build a consumer proposition; keep B2B supply as the route.. Cost: 20000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T2: Do not build a differentiated consumer proposition now. Keep the B2B cable and connection core. Only run the proposed brand-premium test (X1) if leadership wants to examine the consumer option, and treat the result as the gate. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: likely.

Recommendation: Do not build a differentiated consumer proposition now. Keep the B2B cable and connection core. Run the proposed brand-premium test (X1) only if leadership wants to examine the consumer option, and treat its result as the gate. The evidence so far does not show that individuals pay a premium for a Lapp-made product. Target customer: No consumer segment is recommended yet. If the test is run, the target is private EV owners buying home charging (German market, proposed).. Value proposition: None established. The only candidate is a safety and reliability signal from an industrial cable maker (T1), which is unproven.. Favoured theory: T2. Next action: Decide whether to spend the proposed EUR 20,000 and 8 weeks on test X1. If not, record that the consumer option was considered and rejected on current evidence, and keep the B2B route.. Uncertainty: I found that Lapp Mobility sells a wallbox and accessories to private customers through its shop, and that home charging is the main charging place for 63 percent of German e-car drivers in one E.ON-commissioned survey. I found no sales volumes, prices, margins or customer data for the consumer line, and no evidence on whether buyers pay for brand or safety. The trade article supports price competition in the sector, but it is not sales data. The 2026 survey date and its commissioner's interest also need caution. Non-public financial and contractual detail is unknown to me.. Would change if: Lapp's shop data shows the branded product sells at a price above comparable generic wallboxes; The X1 test shows branded listings convert at least 20 percent more than generic listings at equal price, and keep at least 80 percent of conversion at a +10 percent price; Buyer surveys cite safety or brand as the main purchase reason; Lapp discloses consumer sales volumes or margins that are material to the group. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: likely.

events.text: Objective: Decide whether Krones AG should invest in a differentiated consumer-facing proposition for one specific use case, beyond its B2B filling, packaging and process-technology lines. Identify the option with the highest expected value to shareholders for a bounded test cost, and the evidence that would justify it.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no contact with the company and no knowledge of its intentions; Search budget is limited, so evidence must be chosen carefully; Test budget of EUR 20000 and a 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Financial and contractual detail may be non-public; state what could not be found; About 90 percent of sales are abroad and customers are beverage, liquid-food, food, chemical, cosmetics and pharmaceutical producers, so any consumer move must be justified against that core. Alternatives: No expansion: keep the current B2B machinery and service model and add nothing for consumers; Product redesign: scale existing filling or packaging technology into a smaller product for one consumer use case; Different route to existing buyers: a brand-facing or on-site service sold through the same customers, such as refill or line-as-a-service; Different customer group: a niche end-user segment such as craft brewers or small-batch producers, using Steinecker brewhouse know-how; Consumer software or data product: monetise process know-how through monitoring or design tools for small producers; Licensing or partnership: a consumer brand or appliance maker takes the product to market and Krones earns a royalty on its technology.
Searched for "Krones consumer home appliance"; found krones-picobrew-shutdown, krones-home-brew-machine-market, krones-lg-homebrew.

T1: Households will pay a premium for a home appliance that brews fresh beer on demand from capsules, because it removes the time, skill and cleaning burden of homebrewing. A machine maker that controls the capsule consumables can earn recurring margin on each brew. Who benefits: Households who want fresh, varied beer without the work of brewing; the appliance maker, through recurring capsule sales. Why behaviour changes: Homebrewing is slow (about two weeks per batch in the LG example) and messy. A capsule appliance turns it into a convenience purchase, so the buyer pays for time saved and for variety, and then keeps buying consumables.. How value is captured: Recurring sales of proprietary capsules at high margin, on top of a one-off appliance price (LG example: about 3.99 million won, USD 3,386, per set-up). Assumptions: Buyers accept a high up-front appliance price; Consumable margins stay high enough to cover appliance support; Capsule recipes can be protected or are hard to copy; Repeat purchase rates are high enough for lifetime value to exceed acquisition cost. Predictions: Households pay for convenience and variety more than for cost saving, so willingness to pay rises with time saved per batch; Capsule repeat purchase stays high after the first three months; Sales concentrate in households already buying craft beer.

T2: Consumer home-brewing appliances fail because the hardware maker has no consumer brand, channel or ongoing service, and the value goes to whoever owns the customer relationship. A B2B machine maker like Krones would capture little value unless it licenses its technology to a consumer brand. Who benefits: Consumer brands and appliance retailers that own the buyer relationship and recurring consumable sales; the hardware maker captures only a royalty or component fee. Why behaviour changes: Buyers buy from trusted brands and recurring sources. A machine without an ongoing supply of ingredients, software and support gives buyers reasons to stop buying, which the PicoBrew shutdown illustrates: a device-only business that could not sustain itself.. How value is captured: A consumer brand or retailer earns margin on consumables and subscriptions; Krones earns a licence fee or component margin, not consumer margin. Assumptions: Consumer appliance value depends on brand trust, distribution and service more than on process engineering; A hardware-only maker cannot fund long-term support and consumables; Krones has no consumer brand or retail channel in public evidence. Predictions: Device makers that lack consumables or subscriptions exit or enter receivership more often; Successful home brewing products are sold by consumer brands or companies with a retail channel; Krones-type industrial makers appear in consumer products only as licensed component or technology suppliers.

T1 supports, from krones-lg-homebrew (company_assertion): "Each set of capsules - different capsules contain different ingredients - can make 5 liters, or about 10.5 pints, of beer after roughly two weeks of brewing.". Does not show: This is a product description of one LG appliance in a news article, not evidence that households buy it or repeat-buy capsules. It gives a price (3.99 million won, USD 3,386) but no sales, volumes, margins or repeat-purchase rates, so it cannot show willingness to pay or that consumable margins hold..

T2 supports, from krones-picobrew-shutdown (market_fact): "PicoBrew, the homebrewing appliance startup based in Seattle, is effectively shutting down". Does not show: The excerpt does not give the cause of the shutdown, so it cannot show that the lack of a consumer brand, channel or consumables was the reason. It is one failed device company, not a test of whether hardware-only makers always fail, and it says nothing about Krones..

Looked for evidence against T2: "home brewing appliance sold through retail with consumables or subscription succeeded without consumer brand"; found krones-lg-homebrew, krones-home-brew-machine-market, krones-speidel-braumeister.

T2 contradicts, from krones-speidel-braumeister (company_assertion): "It is the ideal brewing device for switching from hobby to commercial brewing, for example as an introduction for caterers who want to offer their own beer to their guests.". Does not show: This is the maker's own marketing claim. It does not show sales volume, profitability or that Speidel sells to households rather than caterers, and it does not show how long the company has operated. It is a counterexample to the claim that hardware-only makers cannot sustain a business, but only for a hobby-to-commercial product, and it does not prove a consumer brand is unnecessary..

Test "Paid pre-order and capsule-subscription test for a home beer appliance concept" between T1; T2. Method: Run a landing page in Germany offering a refundable EUR deposit on a capsule beer appliance at a proposed price, with an opt-in for a capsule subscription. Separately, send a short licensing enquiry to 15 consumer brands and appliance retailers asking whether they would take the technology and sell it under their brand. Proposed design, not yet run.. Sample: Proposed: about 2000 landing-page visitors recruited from homebrewing and craft-beer channels, and 15 licensing prospects. Measure: Deposit conversion rate on the appliance, share opting into a recurring capsule subscription, and number of brand partners agreeing to a licensing discussion. Predictions: T1: Deposit conversion is high enough at the proposed price, and a large share opt into the capsule subscription, so the appliance and consumables can carry a recurring margin.; T2: Direct deposit conversion is low or subscription opt-in is weak, while several brands show interest in licensing, so value sits with the brand owner rather than the hardware maker.. Decision rule: Proceed to a prototype only if deposit conversion is at least 3 percent of visitors (proposed threshold) and at least 40 percent of depositors opt into the capsule subscription. If conversion is below 1 percent and at least 3 brand partners show licensing interest, pursue licensing instead. Otherwise stop.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T2: Do not build a Krones-branded consumer appliance now. Treat consumer home brewing as a licensing or partnership option to test cheaply, and keep the core B2B business as it is. Run the proposed pre-order and licensing test before committing any product development money. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not build a Krones-branded consumer home-brewing appliance now. Keep the core B2B business as it is. If the company wants a consumer option, test licensing or partnership with a consumer brand first, at low cost, before any product development. This rests on thin evidence and is a hypothesis to test, not a finding. Target customer: No consumer customer is established. The only candidate segment in the evidence is households and hobby brewers buying home beer appliances, and the evidence on their willingness to pay is absent.. Value proposition: Krones would supply brewing or filling technology and take a licence fee or component margin. A consumer brand would own the buyer, the consumables and the service.. Favoured theory: T2. Next action: Run the proposed 8-week, EUR 15,000 pre-order and licensing test (X1, proposed, not run). Before that, check what Krones and its Steinecker brand already sell to individual buyers, because my searches did not find this.. Uncertainty: I could not establish from public sources whether Krones already sells anything to individual buyers; my search for a Krones consumer product returned nothing about Krones. Financial and contractual detail, including any licensing terms, is not public. The market figure comes from a vendor research report, not an independent study, and is not dated. Only three consumer-facing sources were read, and none shows household demand, repeat purchase or margins. The PicoBrew shutdown does not give its cause. The Speidel source is the maker's own marketing claim. T1 and T2 are both unresolved.. Would change if: Krones or Steinecker already sells to individual buyers at scale, which would make a direct route more credible; The pre-order test shows deposit conversion at or above 3 percent with at least 40 percent opting into capsule subscriptions, which would support T1 and a direct product; Several consumer brands express real licensing interest and none shows direct demand, which would confirm T2; Independent data showing household capsule repeat purchase, or the cause of PicoBrew's failure pointing to hardware economics rather than channel, would change the weighting; Krones's own disclosures show a consumer segment or a licensing business already in place. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

case.question: Should TOMRA Systems ASA develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing reverse vending machines for deposit return systems and sensor-based sorting machines for retailers, deposit system operators, recyclers, mining companies and food processors? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 72 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Bag drop is a convenient collection method whereby consumers can drop off entire bags of empty beverage containers at collection points and have their deposit refunded. It is a well-established and popular complement to reverse vending machines and redemption centers in North America, with strong growth potential.

With no retailer obligation in the New South Wales’ DRS, TOMRA saw value in a consumer app that could instead offer digital payout of refunds, and a map to show recyclers where to return their containers.

Supermarkets, grocery stores, convenience stores and newsagents that sell drinks in the scheme must host a return point for drinks containers, unless they qualify for an exemption. The return point can be manual or automated using a reverse vending machine.

events.text: Objective: Decide whether TOMRA should build a differentiated consumer-facing proposition for a specific use case, beyond its B2B reverse vending and sorting machines, and identify what public evidence would justify that investment.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no company contact or insider knowledge of intentions; Existing reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be established before theorising; Test budget of 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Search budget is limited (7 searches left); one search is kept for challenge; Financial and contractual detail may be non-public and must be flagged as a gap; Simulated results cannot be cited as evidence. Alternatives: No expansion: keep the current B2B and deposit-system model and invest only in core RVM and sorting products; Product redesign: adapt existing machines for a consumer-facing use such as a smaller home or in-store unit, sold through current channels; Consumer service route: provide return access to individuals via retailers or apps, with TOMRA as platform rather than device seller; Different customer group: target municipalities, brand owners or food processors with a use-case-specific offering rather than individuals; Partnership or licensing: supply sensing technology to a consumer appliance or waste-sorting maker that owns the individual relationship; Targeted pilot in one use case and one market before any product commitment.
Searched for "TOMRA consumer reverse vending home"; found tomra-clynk-bag-drop, tomra-uk-drs-return-points, tomra-mytomra-nsw-origin.

T1: Households will pay for or use a digital return service (app-based payout, locating return points, bag-drop collection) because it removes the time and hassle of counting and carrying containers. Where a scheme does not oblige retailers to host return points, a platform that aggregates refunds and collection can capture value from the operator or brand-owner side. Who benefits: Households with many containers who value time saving; deposit system operators and producers who need collection rates; TOMRA as platform owner that captures fees or data.. Why behaviour changes: Current return effort (sorting, counting, travelling to a machine) is a cost. A digital payout or bag-drop removes part of that cost, so more containers are returned and more refunds are claimed when the service is convenient.. How value is captured: TOMRA earns from operators or brand owners who pay per collected container or per service, and possibly from app usage data. Consumers pay nothing directly.. Assumptions: Return rates in deposit schemes are limited by convenience rather than by lack of deposit value; Operators or producers will pay a service fee for higher collection rates; Consumers will use an app for refunds when no retailer obligation exists; Bag-drop volumes are driven by household convenience rather than by deposit size. Predictions: In markets with an app-based payout, return rates or refund claims per capita rise relative to comparable markets without one; Consumers who use bag-drop return a larger share of containers than those using in-store machines; Operators pay more per container for a service that boosts return rates than for a machine alone.

T2: Households do not return containers mainly because of effort. They hold containers because the deposit value is too small to motivate a trip. A consumer product that raises the value per return, for example by bundling refunds into a donation or a loyalty credit, would change behaviour more than convenience alone, and a manufacturer that owns the refund mechanism could capture a share of that value. Who benefits: Households that hold containers; charities or retailers that receive donated or credited refunds; TOMRA if it captures a fee on the refund mechanism.. Why behaviour changes: A small deposit makes a return trip seem not worth it. If the refund is donated or converted into a larger reward, the perceived value of each return rises, so more people make the trip.. How value is captured: TOMRA earns a transaction or platform fee on refund routing, or sells the machine and software that enables donation or credit at the point of return.. Assumptions: Deposit value per container is small relative to the perceived cost of returning it; Donation or credit options raise perceived value enough to change return behaviour; Retailers or charities will pay for or accept the routing; Return rates are not already near saturation in mature schemes. Predictions: Return rates rise when refunds can be donated or credited, compared with cash-only refunds in the same scheme; Share of deposits donated rises when donation is the default option at the machine; Effect is larger in schemes with low deposit values than in schemes with high deposit values.

T1 supports, from tomra-mytomra-nsw-origin (company_assertion): "With no retailer obligation in the New South Wales’ DRS, TOMRA saw value in a consumer app that could instead offer digital payout of refunds, and a map to show recyclers where to return their containers.". Does not show: This is TOMRA's own account of why it built the app. It does not show that households returned more containers, or that operators paid for the service. The headline 10 million user sessions measures app use, not return rates or willingness to pay..

T2 neutral, from tomra-clynk-bag-drop (company_assertion): "Bag drop is a convenient collection method whereby consumers can drop off entire bags of empty beverage containers at collection points and have their deposit refunded.". Does not show: This is a company's description of a collection method in North America. It says nothing about deposit value, donation or credit options, or whether a small deposit limits returns. It frames the service as convenience, which is the rival cause in T1, not the value-per-return cause in T2. It is also a company claim, not a measured return rate..
Looked for evidence against T1: "return rates deposit scheme convenience did not increase digital refund app"; found tomra-mytomra-nsw-origin, tomra-uk-drs-return-points, tomra-mytomra-app.

Test "Convenience versus value-per-return pilot at existing machine sites" between T1; T2. Method: Randomised pilot across sites in one deposit-scheme market where TOMRA or a partner already runs machines. Sites are split into three arms for 12 weeks: (a) control with cash refund only; (b) convenience arm with digital payout and a return-point map added; (c) value arm with a donation or credit option added at the machine. Container counts and app or donation uptake are logged per site. Scheme terms are not changed.. Sample: Proposed: 30 sites, 10 per arm, selected to be comparable on footfall. Estimated 150 to 200 weekly active returners per site.. Measure: Containers returned per site per week, relative to the control arm's baseline in weeks 1 to 2. Secondary: share of refunds taken as digital payout or donation.. Predictions: T1: The convenience arm raises returns per site by a larger margin than the value arm, because the cost of returning falls rather than the reward rising.; T2: The value arm raises returns per site by a larger margin than the convenience arm, because the reward per return rises rather than the cost of returning falling.. Decision rule: Back T1 if the convenience arm's uplift is at least 1.5 times the value arm's uplift and both are above 5 percent over control. Back T2 if the reverse holds by the same margin. If neither arm clears 5 percent, or the two uplifts are within 1.5 times of each other, neither theory is supported and the investment case stays unproven.. Cost: 18000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not commit to a consumer product yet. T1 (convenience, via digital payout and bag-drop collection, captured through operator and platform fees) is the better-supported lead, but the evidence is company claims only. Run the proposed pilot before any product investment, and treat the consumer route as unproven. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: unlikely.

T1 revised: SIMULATED, hypothetical only, not real data. If this result were real, it would weaken the simple form of T1. The doorstep-collection offer, which removes the most effort, got fewer active sign-ups after 30 days (32) than the store drop-off offer (72). So reducing effort alone does not explain uptake. The result also does not test deposit value (T2), and it is limited to one recruited group, so it does not decide between the theories. Under this what-if, T1 would need a narrower claim: the return trip and its fit with routine matter, not only how little effort it takes. New claim: Households take up a return service when it fits an existing routine such as a store trip, not necessarily when it removes all effort. Platform value comes from routing and payout, with operator fees as the capture mechanism. Whether doorstep collection pays at any fee is unproven.. Evidence: SYN-TOMRA-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Do not commit capital to a new consumer product yet. TOMRA already reaches individuals indirectly, through the myTOMRA refund app in New South Wales and the bag-drop collection business it acquired in the northeastern US. Test whether convenience or value per return drives returns before any product investment. Treat the consumer route as a service extension of existing channels, not a new device line. Target customer: Deposit scheme operators and brand owners who pay for collection rates, with households as end users of a refund or collection service. Individuals are reached indirectly, not sold a device.. Value proposition: A refund and collection service that raises return rates through digital payout, return-point routing and possibly bag-drop, with TOMRA earning fees from operators or producers. Its value depends on evidence not yet gathered.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed 12-week randomised pilot (X1, estimated 18000 EUR, 30 proposed sites in one scheme market) comparing a cash-only control, a convenience arm and a value arm. Back T1 if the convenience uplift is at least 1.5 times the value uplift and both exceed 5 percent over control. First confirm an operator will host the sites and share return counts.. Uncertainty: High. Evidence is company claims or general government guidance. I found no independent return-rate data, app revenue, fee figures, operator contract terms or bag-drop volumes. The app figure counts sessions, not returns. A challenge search found no contrary study, but also no supporting one. One simulated result was read as a what-if and is excluded from the evidence.. Would change if: Independent data showing return rates are unchanged where app or convenience refunds were added, weakening T1; Pilot value-arm uplift at least 1.5 times the convenience uplift, moving belief to T2; Operators will not pay a per-container or service fee, removing the capture mechanism; Disclosed figures showing app or bag-drop revenue large enough to justify funding; No partner operator will host pilot sites, making the test infeasible. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: unlikely.

case.question: Should Brembo N.V. develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing brake systems for vehicle manufacturers and replacement parts for the aftermarket? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: The brakes bring 50 years of motorsport heritage, a little Italian flare, buckets of power and market-leading adjustability to mountain biking, but they come at a price (€750 for the kit) that’s going to be tricky to justify.
Type-approval to R90 is required for all replacement brake linings throughout the European Union and in non-European countries that have adopted ECE Regulations.

The new XTRA Signature disc also makes its debut, developed for urban and everyday use. Finally, the offer extends to the off-road segment with the first Brembo braking solutions dedicated to Side-by-Side Vehicles (SSVs).

The Brembo Expert workshop network, that as of today exceeds the one thousand mark in the national and international territory, is capable of offering a professional and cutting edge service for every kind of vehicle.

Designed and tested specifically for track day enthusiasts and for drivers who demand maximum performance from their vehicle, these systems offer exceptional performance along with a truly sporty look.

Their compact and lightweight design helps reduce the unsprung weight, significantly improving vehicle dynamics. Stability, endurance and consistency: every detail is designed for motorbike enthusiasts seeking uncompromising performance.

Overall, the performance and accessory aftermarket continues to show strong results, as roughly one-fourth of drivers purchased products within the industry to personalize their vehicles last year. The Upgrade braking systems solutions are designed specifically for wholesalers and distributors to meet this demand.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Brembo N.V. should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current brake systems and aftermarket replacement parts, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.. Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Need to identify a specific consumer use case with clear demand and a viable route to market.; Evidence must demonstrate consumer willingness to pay and a viable business model for Brembo.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., performance brake kits for hobbyists, racing enthusiasts, or custom builds).; 2) Expand the aftermarket by offering premium replacement parts or service contracts for individual consumers.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing on B2B brake systems and aftermarket parts without new consumer offerings.; 4) Partner with existing consumer brands to co‑brand brake components for individual buyers (e.g., limited‑edition disc kits).; 5) Target a new consumer segment such as electric vehicle (EV) owners with specialized brake systems..
Searched for "Brembo consumer products individual buyers"; found brembo-sema-aftermarket, brembo-bikeradar-review, brembo-eicma-aftermarket.
Searched for "Brembo aftermarket replacement parts consumer"; found brembo-sema-aftermarket, brembo-ece-r90, brembo-expert-workshops.
Searched for "Brembo consumer market demand individual buyers"; found brembo-sema-aftermarket, brembo-gt-kit, brembo-upgrade-wholesale.

Searched for "Brembo racing enthusiasts performance brake kits"; found brembo-gt-kit, brembo-bikeradar-review, brembo-moto-upgrade-calipers.
Searched for "Brembo aftermarket sales revenue"; found brembo-sema-aftermarket, brembo-shimano-inventory, brembo-ziv-bike-decline.

T1: Performance-oriented individual buyers will purchase Brembo brake kits for their vehicles because they seek superior braking performance and a sporty aesthetic, and they are willing to pay a premium for heritage and performance. Who benefits: Track day enthusiasts, racing enthusiasts, and high-performance car owners who value performance and style.. Why behaviour changes: These buyers perceive Brembo as a symbol of performance and status, and they are willing to invest in a kit that offers measurable performance gains and a distinctive look.. How value is captured: Brembo can capture value by selling premium-priced kits directly to consumers through its lifestyle collection and e-commerce platform, and by leveraging its brand reputation for performance.. Assumptions: There is a significant segment of individual buyers who actively seek performance upgrades for their vehicles.; These buyers are willing to pay a premium price for Brembo products.; Brembo can effectively reach and convert this segment through its lifestyle brand and online channels.. Predictions: A survey of performance-oriented individual buyers will show a high percentage (e.g., 60% or more) indicating they would purchase a Brembo brake kit.; Sales of Brembo lifestyle kits will generate higher revenue than standard aftermarket parts.; Brand awareness among this segment will be higher than among the general consumer base..

T2: Brembo will expand its consumer proposition by offering a differentiated line of brake kits and lifestyle accessories for individual buyers, because the company already has a strong brand reputation for performance and heritage, and it can capture value through premium pricing and direct-to-consumer sales. Who benefits: Individual buyers who value performance, heritage, and style, and Brembo itself through higher margins and brand extension.. Why behaviour changes: These buyers are already familiar with Brembo's performance credentials and seek products that reflect their status and passion for performance, making them willing to purchase premium kits and lifestyle items.. How value is captured: Brembo can capture value by selling differentiated kits and lifestyle products directly to consumers at premium prices, leveraging its existing distribution channels and brand equity to command higher margins.. Assumptions: There is a segment of individual buyers who are willing to pay a premium for Brembo products.; Brembo can effectively reach this segment through its lifestyle collection and e-commerce platform.; The premium pricing model is feasible without significantly eroding market share in its B2B segments.. Predictions: A survey of individual buyers will show a significant percentage (e.g., 40% or more) indicating they would purchase a Brembo brake kit.; Sales of the differentiated lifestyle kits will generate higher revenue than standard aftermarket parts.; Brand awareness among individual buyers will increase when exposed to Brembo's lifestyle offerings..

T1 supports, from brembo-bikeradar-review (independent_study): "The brakes bring 50 years of motorsport heritage, a little Italian flare, buckets of power and market-leading adjustability to mountain biking, but they come at a price (€750 for the kit) that’s going to be tricky to justify.". Does not show: The review does not provide data on actual purchase intent, willingness to pay, or the size of the target segment of performance-oriented individual buyers..

T2 supports, from brembo-eicma-aftermarket (company_assertion): "The new XTRA Signature disc also makes its debut, developed for urban and everyday use.". Does not show: The source does not provide evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or the size of the target segment of individual buyers..
Looked for evidence against T1: "Brembo brake kit consumer price sensitivity demand"; found brembo-bikeradar-review, brembo-gt-kit, brembo-sema-aftermarket.

Test "Digital Messaging Test for Performance Brake Kit" between T1; T2. Method: Run a targeted digital ad campaign with two versions: Version A (performance-focused) and Version B (lifestyle-focused). Both ads feature a Brembo brake kit at a premium price (e.g., €1,200). Version A emphasizes heritage, performance, and sporty aesthetics; Version B emphasizes lifestyle, status, and the Brembo lifestyle collection. Track clicks, conversions, and willingness to pay.. Sample: Estimated 5,000 individual buyers in the UK and Germany who have shown interest in performance upgrades (e.g., visited a performance car forum or purchased an upgrade kit in the past 12 months).. Measure: Conversion rate (percentage of visitors who click the buy button) and average willingness to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Version A will generate a higher conversion rate and higher average willingness to pay than Version B, because performance-oriented buyers are more likely to respond to performance messaging.; T2: Version B will generate a higher conversion rate and higher average willingness to pay than Version A, because lifestyle-oriented buyers are more likely to respond to status and brand messaging.. Decision rule: If Version A conversion rate >= 5% and average willingness to pay >= €1,200, proceed with a performance-focused consumer proposition. If Version B conversion rate >= 5% and average willingness to pay >= €1,200, proceed with a lifestyle-focused consumer proposition. If neither condition is met, do not expand into consumer offerings.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Conduct the proposed digital messaging test (X1) to empirically compare performance and lifestyle messaging. If Version A meets the conversion and willingness-to-pay thresholds, proceed with a performance-focused consumer proposition; if Version B meets thresholds, proceed with a lifestyle-focused proposition. If neither meets thresholds, do not expand into consumer offerings at this time. The test will provide theEv Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Run the proposed digital messaging test (X1) to empirically compare performance and lifestyle messaging. If Version A meets the conversion and willingness-to-pay thresholds, proceed with a performance-focused consumer proposition; if Version B meets thresholds, proceed with a lifestyle-focused proposition. If neither meets thresholds, do not expand into consumer offerings at this time. Target customer: Performance-oriented individual buyers (e.g., track day enthusiasts, racing enthusiasts, and high-performance car owners) who value superior braking performance and a sporty aesthetic.. Value proposition: A differentiated brake kit that combines Brembo's heritage, performance heritage, and market-leading adjustability, sold at a premium price through Brembo's lifestyle collection and e-commerce platform.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the digital messaging test (X1) within the 12-week timeline and 20,000 EUR budget, analyzing conversion rates and willingness to pay to decide whether to pursue a performance-focused or lifestyle-focused consumer proposition.. Uncertainty: The size of the target segment of individual buyers, their willingness to pay a premium price, and the competitive landscape for performance brake kits are uncertain. The test will provide empirical evidence to resolve these uncertainties.. Would change if: If the test shows Version A (performance-focused) achieving a conversion rate of at least 5% and an average willingness to pay of at least €1,200, the recommendation would shift to proceed with a performance-focused consumer proposition.; If the test shows Version B (lifestyle-focused) achieving a conversion rate of at least 5% and an average willingness to pay of at least €1,200, the recommendation would shift to proceed with a lifestyle-focused consumer proposition.; If neither version meets the thresholds, the recommendation would remain to not expand into consumer offerings at this time.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

case.question: Should Kardex Holding AG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing automated storage and retrieval systems (vertical lift modules, carousels and AutoStore-based systems) for warehouses, factories and organisations? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 letters of intent for the rental offer and 32 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
Kardex only permits factory-trained, certified personnel to install and service our equipment.

Kardex Remstar has subsidiaries throughout Europe, Middle East/Africa, Asia-Pacific and the US. For Kardex Remstar, the combination of local presence with a global sales and service organization has become a crucial differentiator in terms of securing and gaining market share.

Kardex automated storage systems bring speed, structure, and visibility to dealership parts departments. They condense storage footprints, increase on-hand inventory, and allow service operations to run more efficiently—resulting in faster repairs, higher throughput, and increased customer satisfaction.
Kardex has been a significant name in business data storage since 1898, tracing back to the Rand Ledger Company.

Kardex provides an intelligent entry into automation with its dynamic storage and retrieval systems, offers integrated material handling systems, small parts storage systems including multi-shuttle technology, and automated high-bay warehouses.
When looking at facility size, the report found that the larger the facility or company, the more likely it is to adopt RaaS.
Kardex Remstar customers can be found in a broad range of industries, from highly industrialized through to office environments.

T1: Individual homeowners and small businesses will adopt automated storage systems if they perceive a clear, measurable benefit that directly reduces their storage costs or improves space utilization, because they are price-sensitive and value tangible returns on investment. Who benefits: Homeowners and small business owners who currently store items manually and incur high storage costs or limited space.. Why behaviour changes: They would change from manual storage to automated storage if they can demonstrate a cost savings or space efficiency that is quantifiable and easy to understand, such as reduced rental costs or increased usable space.. How value is captured: Kardex would capture value by selling a differentiated consumer product (e.g., a compact, affordable vertical lift module) and offering a subscription or service model for maintenance and performance monitoring.. Assumptions: There is a measurable cost savings or space efficiency that can be communicated to consumers.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product that directly reduces their storage costs.; Kardex can produce or license a product that meets consumer expectations for size, safety, and ease of use.. Predictions: In a test offering a consumer product with a clear cost-saving claim, purchase intent or pre-orders will be higher than a control offering a generic B2B product.; Surveyed consumers will rank cost savings as the top reason for purchasing, with a higher willingness to pay for a product that promises a measurable return on investment..

T2: Individual homeowners and small businesses will adopt automated storage systems if they perceive a lifestyle or convenience benefit that aligns with modern living patterns, such as easy access to stored items, reduced clutter, or integration with smart home ecosystems, because they value convenience and status. Who benefits: Homeowners and small business owners who prioritize convenience, organization, and modern living.. Why behaviour changes: They would change from manual storage to automated storage if the system offers features like remote access, automated retrieval, or seamless integration with smart devices, making storage feel like a modern convenience rather than a cost.. How value is captured: Kardex would capture value by positioning a consumer product as a lifestyle upgrade, offering premium features (e.g., touchscreen interfaces, app integration) and potentially a subscription for software updates and support.. Assumptions: Consumers associate automated storage with modern convenience and status.; Smart home integration is a meaningful differentiator for this segment.; Kardex can develop or license features that meet these lifestyle expectations without major product redesign.. Predictions: In a test offering a lifestyle-focused product, purchase intent will be higher than a control offering a functional B2B product.; Surveyed consumers will rank convenience and status as the top reasons for purchasing, with a higher willingness to pay for a product that feels like a modern convenience..

Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Cost Savings vs. Convenience" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offers. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a cost-saving proposition (e.g., 'Save EUR 200/year on storage costs with our compact vertical lift module') and a functional description of the product. Group B sees a convenience proposition (e.g., 'Easy access to stored items with remote control and app integration'). Both groups see the same product details and a call to pre-order or purchase.. Sample: 500 adults aged 25-55, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and geographic region to ensure representativeness.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: pre-order or purchase) and willingness to pay (maximum amount willing to pay).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group B, because the cost-saving message directly addresses a measurable financial benefit.; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group A, because the convenience message aligns with modern living patterns and status.. Decision rule: If Group A's purchase intent is at least 15 percentage points higher than Group B's, conclude T1 is more supported. If Group B's purchase intent is at least 15 percentage points higher than Group A, conclude T2 is more supported. If the difference is below 15 percentage points, both theories remain equally supported and further testing is needed.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes measurable cost savings and space efficiency, targeting homeowners and small businesses. Test "Consumer Messaging Test for Assistive vs Lifestyle Home Automation" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of consumers with and without mobility impairments. Participants view a product description of a home automation device (e.g., a smart cane or posture support system) and are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: (1) Medical necessity framing (emphasizing rehabilitation and mobility support) or (2) Lifestyle framing (emphasizing status, convenience, and modern living). After viewing the description, participants indicate their willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale and their purchase intent (1‑10).. Sample: 300 participants (150 with mobility impairments, 150 without) recruited via an online panel, balanced across both message conditions.. Measure: Average willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent (1‑10) for each message condition.. Predictions: T1: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in the medical necessity condition compared to the lifestyle condition.; T2: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in the lifestyle condition compared to the medical necessity condition.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the medical necessity condition is at least 1.5 points higher than the average WTP for the lifestyle condition, conclude T1 is supported. If the average WTP for the lifestyle condition is at least 1.5 points higher than the average WTP for the medical necessity condition, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, the results are inconclusive and further testing is recommended.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

case.question: Should TOMRA Systems ASA develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing reverse vending machines for deposit return systems and sensor-based sorting machines for retailers, deposit system operators, recyclers, mining companies and food processors? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 32 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Bag drop is a convenient collection method whereby consumers can drop off entire bags of empty beverage containers at collection points and have their deposit refunded. It is a well-established and popular complement to reverse vending machines and redemption centers in North America, with strong growth potential.

Member States are required to set up a deposit return system for beverage cans and plastic bottles in order to reach a 90% collection for recycling target by 2029. Exemptions may be issued to a Member State that has achieved 80% collection by 2026.
myTOMRA makes recycling more fun and convenient than ever before. Collect your recyclables, return them to your nearest recycling point and collect your digital refunds.
Reached a new milestone of 10 million user sessions and the equivalent of 50 million euros paid in deposit refunds

With no retailer obligation in the New South Wales’ DRS, TOMRA saw value in a consumer app that could instead offer digital payout of refunds, and a map to show recyclers where to return their containers.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify TOMRA Systems ASA investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings.. Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.; Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a clear path to capture value for individual consumers.; Any recommendation must consider TOMRA’s existing B2B customers and current product portfolio.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a consumer proposition targeting individual households (e.g., home recycling for single‑use containers).; 2) Expand B2B offerings by targeting new segments such as small retailers, food processors, or mining companies with additional sorting or recycling solutions.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing on existing B2B markets without new consumer initiatives.; 4) License TOMRA’s sensor‑based sorting technology to third‑party consumer brands for integrated recycling solutions..
Searched for "TOMRA Systems consumer individual households home recycling"; found tomra-mytomra-nsw-origin, tomra-eu-ppwr-drs, tomra-clynk-bag-drop.
Searched for "TOMRA consumer app digital payout refund individual households"; found tomra-mytomra-nsw-origin, tomra-mytomra-app, tomra-mytomra-milestone.

T1: Households will adopt home recycling for single‑use containers if TOMRA’s consumer app provides real, immediate digital refunds rather than relying on traditional redemption centers or bag‑drop systems. Who benefits: Individual consumers gain convenience and instant cash; TOMRA captures recurring revenue through digital refunds and may increase collection volumes.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers currently must travel to redemption centers or bag‑drop points for refunds; the app eliminates that friction and makes recycling feel rewarding through digital payout.. How value is captured: TOMRA earns per‑transaction fees or subscription fees from digital refunds, and can use data on container types to improve sorting efficiency and lower costs.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a small fee for digital refunds.; TOMRA can integrate digital refund processing into its existing systems without significant hardware changes.; Regulatory requirements allow digital payout of refunds in target markets.. Predictions: A pilot offering the app in a single market will achieve at least 5% of target households downloading the app within 3 months.; Average refund value will be at least €0.50, with a conversion rate of at least 10% of collected containers processed through the app..

T2: Households will adopt home recycling for single‑use containers if TOMRA’s sensor‑based sorting machines reduce the cost of recycling for retailers and food processors, making it cheaper to collect and process containers than current methods. Who benefits: Retailers and food processors gain lower recycling costs and improved supply chain efficiency; TOMRA captures value through higher volume sales of sorting machines and potential licensing of its sensor technology.. Why behaviour changes: Current recycling methods (e.g., bag drops, redemption centers) are expensive for retailers and food processors; sensor‑based sorting lowers labor and material costs, making recycling more profitable and attractive.. How value is captured: TOMRA earns per‑unit sales of sorting machines and can license its sensor technology to other retailers, generating recurring revenue and market expansion.. Assumptions: Retailers and food processors are willing to invest in sensor‑based sorting if it reduces their recycling costs.; TOMRA can scale its sensor technology to meet the needs of multiple retailers and food processors.; Regulatory requirements do not prohibit the use of sensor‑based sorting in the target markets.. Predictions: A pilot deployment of sensor‑based sorting in a single retail or food‑processing facility will achieve at least 15% reduction in recycling costs compared to current methods within 6 months.; At least 20% of target retailers or food processors will express interest in purchasing the sensor‑based sorting system within 12 months..

T1 supports, from tomra-mytomra-app (company_assertion): "myTOMRA makes recycling more fun and convenient than ever before.". Does not show: The source does not provide data on digital refund uptake, conversion rates, or willingness to pay; it only states a stated intent to make recycling convenient..

T2 supports, from tomra-eu-ppwr-drs (regulation): "Member States are required to set up a deposit return system for beverage cans and plastic bottles in order to reach a 90% collection for recycling target by 2029.". Does not show: The source does not address the cost savings of sensor-based sorting for retailers or food processors; it only outlines EU regulatory requirements for deposit return systems..
Looked for evidence against T1: "consumer app digital payout refund low adoption household"; found tomra-mytomra-nsw-origin, tomra-mytomra-app, tomra-mytomra-milestone.

T2 neutral, from tomra-clynk-bag-drop (company_assertion): "Bag drop is a convenient collection method whereby consumers can drop off entire bags of empty beverage containers at collection points and have their deposit refunded.". Does not show: The source describes a traditional bag‑drop system and does not address the cost savings of sensor‑based sorting for retailers or food processors; it only notes the popularity of bag drops as a complement to reverse vending machines..

Test "Digital vs Sensor Pilot Test" between T1; T2. Method: Run a 12‑week pilot in two distinct markets (e.g., NSW, Australia) with identical consumer messaging but different mechanisms: in Market A, households download the myTOMRA app and collect containers via the app; in Market B, households use a sensor‑based bag‑drop system (e.g., C&C Consolidated Holdings). Track app downloads, digital refund uptake, and container return rates.. Sample: 10,000 households per market, recruited via social media and local partnerships, balanced for age, income, and recycling behavior.. Measure: 1) App downloads and active users within 3 months. 2) Average refund value per household (digital payout). 3) Container return rate (percentage of collected containers processed through the app vs. bag drop).. Predictions: T1: Market A will achieve at least 5% app downloads and an average refund value of €0.50, with a return rate of at least 10% of collected containers processed through the app.; T2: Market B will achieve at least 15% reduction in recycling costs for the participating retailer or food processor, and at least 20% of target retailers will express interest in purchasing the sensor‑based sorting system within 12 months.. Decision rule: If Market A meets both the 5% download threshold and the 10% return rate threshold, proceed to develop a consumer app proposition. If Market B meets the 15% cost‑reduction threshold and the 20% interest threshold, invest in a sensor‑based sorting pilot for retailers. If neither threshold is met, do not expand into consumer or B2B channels.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed Digital vs Sensor Pilot Test (X1) to empirically compare household adoption of a digital refund app versus a sensor-based bag‑drop system. The test will determine whether the stated convenience of the app (T1) translates into actual demand, and whether the cost‑saving mechanism (T2) is viable for retailers. If neither threshold is met, do not expand into consumer or B2B channels; otherwise, proceed. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated result (SYN-TOMRA-UPDATE) does not address digital refund mechanisms or household adoption of a consumer app; it tests a different mechanism (doorstep vs store drop-off) and does not provide evidence for or against T1. Therefore T1 remains unchanged. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-TOMRA-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer proposition yet. Run the proposed Digital vs Sensor Pilot Test (X1) to empirically compare household adoption of a digital refund app versus a sensor-based bag‑drop system. If neither threshold is met, do not expand into consumer or B2B channels; otherwise, proceed. Target customer: Individual households in markets where deposit return systems are already in place (e.g., NSW, Australia, EU).. Value proposition: A consumer app that provides real, immediate digital refunds for returned containers, eliminating the need to visit redemption centers or bag‑drop points.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the 12‑week pilot in two markets, tracking app downloads, digital refund uptake, and container return rates against the proposed thresholds.. Uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on household willingness to pay for digital refunds and on the cost‑saving impact of sensor‑based sorting for retailers.. Would change if: If the pilot shows at least 5% app downloads and a 10% return rate, T1 would become more credible and would justify developing a consumer app proposition.; If the pilot shows at least 15% cost reduction for retailers and 20% interest in purchasing sensor‑based sorting, T2 would become more credible and would justify investing in a sensor pilot.; If neither threshold is met, both theories would be weakened and the recommendation would shift to no expansion.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Eberspächer should develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (beyond its OEM/dealer exhaust, heater and thermal business), and what evidence would justify that investment, without assuming the company's intentions.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; company has not asked and nothing describes its intentions; Financial and contractual detail may be non-public; must state what could not be found; Test budget EUR 20,000 and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions; Search budget of 8 total (7 remaining); challenge_theory uses a search; Consumer demand claims from company assertions are not proof of demand. Alternatives: No expansion: remain a B2B supplier to OEMs and specialist dealers; Direct-to-consumer product for a specific use case (e.g., camper/van/overlanding auxiliary heating) using existing heater technology; Aftermarket/retrofit channel via specialist dealers and installers rather than an own consumer brand; Partnership or licensing with a consumer brand or camper-vehicle maker to reach buyers without owning the consumer relationship; Consumer product redesign (e.g., quieter, lower-emission or app-controlled exhaust or heater for enthusiasts); Different customer group: fleet, utility or workshop buyers, or adjacent thermal comfort accessories sold via existing channels.
Searched for "Eberspächer consumer products individual buyers webshop"; found eberspaecher-caravan-salon-2024, autohaus-plant-closures, eberspaecher-boat-heaters.

T1: Leisure owners (campers, caravans, boats) want reliable warmth and dryness in bad weather, and will buy an aftermarket heater through specialist installers and dealers they already trust. Eberspächer can capture value by supplying the product into that existing installer and dealer channel, without owning a consumer brand. Who benefits: Leisure vehicle owners who retrofit heating; specialist installers and dealers who earn fitting margin; Eberspächer, which sells existing heater hardware into a channel it already reaches.. Why behaviour changes: Owners of older or unheated leisure vehicles lack a heater and face condensation and cold. Trade-fair and product marketing (company claims) signal that the product exists for this use, and installers recommend it at the point of sale.. How value is captured: Volume sales of existing heater units and kits to aftermarket installers and dealers at trade margin; little new product development needed.. Assumptions: A meaningful pool of owners of unheated or under-heated leisure vehicles exists and is willing to pay for a retrofit; Installers and dealers stock and recommend Eberspächer units over competitors; Existing heater hardware can be fitted outside OEM integration at acceptable cost and with acceptable installation effort. Predictions: Installer or dealer listings for Eberspächer retrofit heaters in leisure categories can be found in the UK, Germany and Scandinavia; A small paid pilot through 5-10 installers sells units at a rate that covers fitting and margin; Purchases concentrate before autumn and winter and in regions with cold seasons.

T2: Consumers choose their heating when they buy the vehicle, so the purchase decision sits with the vehicle maker and its dealer. A standalone heater brand has little independent pull, and most value stays with OEM fit or is lost to the vehicle sale rather than captured by an Eberspächer consumer proposition. Who benefits: Vehicle makers and their dealers, who keep the heater choice inside the vehicle price; Eberspächer's existing OEM customers, who prefer that Eberspächer not compete with them for end-user attention.. Why behaviour changes: Buyers rarely research heaters as a separate product. They pick a camper, van or boat with heating already specified, so a retrofit product only sells when the factory option is missing or poor.. How value is captured: Eberspächer captures value through OEM supply contracts and factory-fit volumes, not through a consumer brand. A consumer proposition would only earn margin as a niche retrofit, which is small against OEM volume.. Decision rule: Proceed to a larger test only if at least 15 pre-orders come from owners of unheated or under-heated vehicles (5 per cent of enquiries, proposed threshold) and at least 3 of 6 installers commit to stocking. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 72 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1: Private EV owners buy charging cables on safety and reliability grounds, which a cable maker's engineering reputation can win at a premium, so a direct consumer EV-charging accessory line can earn margin. Who benefits: Private EV drivers who want a safe, durable home charging cable; Lapp as seller of a trusted industrial-grade product sold direct to consumers.. Why behaviour changes: Buyers who cannot judge electrical safety by themselves defer to visibly certified, engineering-grade brands, which lifts willingness to pay over generic cheap cables.. How value is captured: Lapp sells a branded, certified cable or wallbox accessory through online or retail channels and keeps the margin that a distributor or electrician would otherwise take.. Assumptions: Private buyers can see or are told the safety and certification difference; Lapp can reach private buyers through online channels at acceptable cost; Price premium is larger than the added channel cost. Predictions: Private buyers in test listings show higher conversion when certification and industrial origin are shown; A price premium of 10 to 20 percent holds without a drop in conversion; Sales concentrate among buyers who already own an EV and have bought a wallbox.

T2: Private EV owners do not choose their own charging cable; the installing electrician or car maker decides, so value sits with the channel that controls installation, and a cable maker captures it only as a component supplier. Who benefits: Installers, wallbox makers and car makers who control the purchase decision; Lapp as a supplier to them.. Why behaviour changes: Buyers defer to the installer or the vehicle bundle because installation is a one-off, technical, and often covered by the car purchase, so they rarely shop for cables themselves.. How value is captured: Lapp earns OEM or wholesale margin by supplying cables and assemblies to wallbox makers and installers, without owning the consumer relationship.. Assumptions: Most private home charging is bought through an installer or bundled with a car or wallbox; Installers and wallbox makers would accept a Lapp component on price and quality; Consumers have little interest in the cable as a separate product. Predictions: Share of private home installations where the buyer chose the cable brand is low; Lapp's sales to wallbox makers would grow faster than any direct-to-consumer line; Consumers asked about cable brand name rank it below installer and car brand.
